concepts.premise: Rank 1 of 12. Ch1 cold open + Ch6 payoff. Suggested Short title: "Every Photo of Hawaii Is Cropped". A postcard of a Big Island beach gets un-cropped: the paper border peels away, the ocean drains, and the beach turns out to be the top of a mountain so heavy it dented the planet. Delivers the film's thesis ("only the tip") in 28 s. Understandable with no context: everyone has seen a Hawaii beach photo.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Every photo of Hawaii is cropped." Frame 0: a paper cut-out postcard (a real PD photo of a Big Island beach on Mauna Loa's flank, e.g. NPS/USGS, VERIFY rights; fallback: our own render with a paper border) fills about 80% of the frame width, tilted 3 degrees. Big printed "HAWAII" across its top (Anton cap 170 px, y 330-500). The same coast is rendered in the engine behind it and lined up with the photo.
concepts.payoff: The counter climbs from the dented true base to the summit and lands on "56,000 FT" (the only number). "From that real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall. Almost twice Everest." The Everest silhouette, on the same base line, reaches about halfway. This is the gasp. Spine facts #2/#3; the narration says "about" and "almost" and names Mauna Loa. Scheduling note: this spends the long-form's climax, so publish it about 7-10 days after the long-form with the long-form as Related Video. Swap the number to 33,500 FT (Mauna Kea, fact #1) only if the showrunner wants to protect the payoff.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Put the ocean back, and / every photo of Hawaii is cropped." The refill rushes up the flank, and the camera eases back up to the beach on the frame-0 keyframe. The paper border flips back in from all four edges (paper-flap SFX), so the last frame is the frame-0 postcard: same camera, same water level, same tilt. Record the last line and the first line as one Rodney take and split it at the seam so the intonation carries over. VO word 1 starts at frame 0. The last word ends 3 frames before the cut. Cut the music at a bar line. No end card.
concepts.beats:
Text zone for every card: x 60-900, y 170-1500.
0.0-2.4 Postcard hook (above).
2.4-4.8 "Here's the rest of the picture." The border peels off and the camera pulls back: the photo was a crop of the real coast. The yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line drops onto the shore with its label (Barlow cap 90).
4.8-9.5 "Drain the ocean, and the beach is the top of a mountain." Live drain with a riser. The camera tilts down with the water. Drowned reef steps break the surface. The basalt slope fills the tall frame.
9.5-13.3 "Keep going. The sea floor isn't the bottom either." The last water sits in the moat at the foot of the slope. Thud.
13.3-18.5 "This mountain is so heavy, it pushed the ocean floor down by miles." Cut-away slice: the crust and Moho sag under the massif (schematic, from the USGS flexure description).
18.5-23.2 "From that real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall." "56,000 FT" counter (Anton cap 280, y 300-580) plus a yellow height bar. Ticks, then an impact on "tall".
23.2-24.6 "Almost twice Everest." The Everest SRTM silhouette slides in on the same base line, label "EVEREST" (cap 100).
24.6-28.0 "Put the ocean back, and..." Refill, push-in, the border flips back on. Loop.
concepts.reuses: The Ch1 0:00 thumbnail-in-motion camera and the HMRG + ETOPO Big Island terrain with the water plane and the SEA LEVEL line. The Ch3 drain to the floor and the Hawaiian Deep moat. The Ch6 11:10 payoff cut-away (crust/Moho sag), the height counter and the Everest SRTM mesh. The Ch6 11:45 refill. New for the Short: the postcard paper card (look-book S10/S12 cut-out style), the vertical tilt-down camera, and the border-flip transition.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: The first line is a provocation every viewer can test against their own memory of Hawaii photos. Each drain step raises the stakes: the beach, then the shore, then the slope, then "the floor isn't the bottom either". The number arrives at 19-23 s. The refill re-crops the picture right as the viewer works out what "cropped" meant, so the replay rewards them: they now see the postcard knowing what is under it. One big number and one continuous camera move, with nothing to skip past.
concepts.probe: There is no Hawaii-only drain Short. The adjacent premises are proven huge: "What If The Ocean Got Flushed?" 23M, "Hawaii Is Much Bigger Than You Think - The Secret Hidden Islands" 14M, "Can You Drain The Atlantic Ocean" 10M, "How Long Is Hawaii, Really?" 7.4M, "How Big is the Biggest Volcano?" 2.6M. The 56,000-ft true height is absent from Shorts: the closest is "The tallest volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa... 9,170" at 1.9K. "Hawaii drained ocean" returns only storm-drain surfing clips and a 28K "What If The Pacific Ocean Drained?". Our edge is a real-bathymetry drain past the sea floor, a number nobody uses, and a postcard device that makes the loop.

concepts.premise: Rank 2 of 12. Ch1 0:14-0:27 (Maui Nui at -400 ft plus the suitcase gag). Suggested title: "You Can't Walk From Maui to Lanai (Unless...)". A paper tourist with a suitcase wants to walk to the next island. We drain 400 ft of ocean, three islands fuse, and he strolls past a beached ferry. Twist: in the last Ice Age this was real. Then the sea comes back and he has to race the tide home.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "You can't walk from Maui to Lanai." Frame 0: low oblique from the West Maui shore looking southwest. Lanai sits on the horizon in the top third, Molokai is at the upper left, and the channel is turquoise. A paper cut-out tourist (real PD traveller photo with a suitcase, NARA/LoC, VERIFY rights) stands at the waterline at centre-left with his feet at y about 1350 and a wave washing over his toes. Labels: "MAUI" by his feet and "LANAI" on the horizon island (Barlow cap 90).
concepts.payoff: The gag comes first: he hops across the dry channel floor past a paper ferry lying on its side on the seabed ("No ferry needed"). The real payoff follows: "And this isn't a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokai and Lanai really were one island." One number: "-400 FT". Spine fact #5 and must-fix #1: Kaho'olawe stays separate and dimmed, and the Penguin Bank lobe surfaces. VERIFY on the HMRG grid that the saddles really surface at -120 to -130 m.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, / you can't walk from Maui to Lanai." During the refill the tourist grabs his suitcase and races back ahead of the rising water. He lands on his frame-0 mark on the Maui shore as the wave reaches his toes. The camera eases onto the frame-0 keyframe and the -400 FT plate rolls back off. The last frame is frame 0. Record the last and first lines as one take and split it at the seam.

Text zone: x 60-900, y 170-1500.
0.0-2.7 Hook (above).
2.7-6.0 "Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean." The "-400 FT" counter rolls in (Anton cap 260, y 260-520). The drain starts on the word "drain" (gurgle plus riser).
6.0-8.0 No VO. Tan banks surface. A yellow rim draws around Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Penguin Bank. Kaho'olawe stays dimmed.
8.0-9.6 "Three islands become one."
9.6-11.6 "No ferry needed." Three squash-and-stretch paper hops across the dry channel, past the beached paper ferry (a PD boat photo).

concepts.reuses: The Ch1 0:14 Maui Nui -400 ft drain shot (the terrain, the yellow rim, Penguin Bank, the dimmed Kaho'olawe), the 0:20 golden-hour pass over the land bridge, and the 0:25 suitcase-tourist gag, rebuilt as a paper cut-out per the look book (no low-poly). New for the Short: the shore-level vertical camera, the beached ferry prop, and the race-the-tide refill.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: It opens with a character, a goal and an obstacle in the first 3 s. The live drain is the solution. The beached ferry is a laugh at 10 s. "This isn't a what-if" flips a gag into a fact at 12 s. The refill creates a chase (will he make it back?) that resolves exactly on the loop line. Every 2-3 s something moves.
concepts.probe: The "Hawaii inter-island travel" premise is proven: "Why Hawaii's Islands Aren't Connected by Boats" 5.4M, "Why You Can't Travel Between Hawaii's Islands by Boat" 181K, "Why Hawaii Isn't Connected by Boats?" 77K, "People Want to Island Hop in Hawaii Without Realizing the Distance" 16K. Lost-land-bridge Shorts pull: Doggerland 806K, 187K and 120K. "Maui Nui" returns zero geology Shorts (only venison and luau clips). Our edge: we drain the real channel live and show a walk where the others show a map and a boat.

concepts.premise: Rank 3 of 12. Ch2 1:20-3:10 (Pali hat gag, Nu'uanu debris field, Manhattan overlay). Suggested title: "Half of This Volcano Is Missing". A tourist at Oahu's windy Pali Lookout loses his hat over the cliff. We follow it out to sea, drain the ocean, and find the other half of the volcano lying on the seafloor in giant blocks. One block is Manhattan-sized, and the hat is sitting on it.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Hold on to your hat." Frame 0: low oblique at the Nu'uanu Pali Lookout on the real Ko'olau terrain, with the stone railing in the foreground. A paper cut-out tourist (real PD photo of a man in a hat, VERIFY rights) stands at the railing with his jacket flapping. Green cliffs fall away to the windward coast, and the ocean fills the top third. Kicker "PALI LOOKOUT, OAHU" (Barlow cap 80, y 220). A wind-gust SFX plays at frame 0 and the hat is already lifting.
concepts.payoff: The blocks surface one after another, then a true-size Manhattan outline (6 px white outline, 55% orange fill) drops from the top of the frame and slams onto the largest block: "One of these pieces is the size of Manhattan." Then the crash zoom: the tiny hat is sitting on the Manhattan block. No big number on screen; the only spoken number is "more than a million years ago". Spine fact #6. VERIFY: measure the block on the HMRG/GLORIA data; if it is much larger, say "bigger than Manhattan" and let the overlay show it.
concepts.loop: Read together: "So next time you're up here, / hold on to your hat. About half of this volcano is missing." From the hat on the block, a 6-frame motion-blurred whip-pan runs back up the cliffs to the lookout. The tourist now wears a new hat and clamps it with both hands, and the wind ramps up. The shot settles on the exact frame-0 camera and pose. On the replay the gust lifts the new hat, so the loop doubles as a gag. Record it as one take and split at the seam.
concepts.beats:
Text zone: x 60-900, y 170-1500.
0.0-1.4 Hook.
1.4-4.0 "About half of this volcano is missing." The hat sails over the edge and the camera follows it out over the cliffs and Kane'ohe Bay.
4.0-7.6 "The rest of it is out there, under the sea." The hat splashes down far offshore. The camera rises to a regional oblique northeast of Oahu.
7.6-12.0 "Drain the ocean, and here it comes. Block after block." Drain to about -4,000 m. A block surfaces about every 1 s with a low thump. The debris field streams away from Oahu.
12.0-15.5 "One of these pieces is the size of Manhattan." The Manhattan outline slams down (impact_deep), label "MANHATTAN" (cap 110).
15.5-23.0 "It all broke off this island more than a million years ago, in one of the biggest landslides on Earth." Pull back so the field and Oahu's sheared windward side share the frame. The scar edge glows yellow for 1 s.
23.0-24.5 No VO. Crash zoom: the hat sits on Manhattan (soft "boop").
24.5-27.5 "So next time you're up here..." Whip back to the lookout and settle on frame 0. Loop.
concepts.reuses: The Ch2 1:20 Pali Lookout hat gag (rebuilt as a paper cut-out), the 1:40-2:20 drain northeast of Oahu with the blocks surfacing, the 2:20 hero shot of the largest block with the true-size Manhattan overlay, and the 2:50 "one of the biggest landslides" line. New for the Short: the hat-follow camera, which is the connecting thread from the cliff to the debris field, and the new-hat loop.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: A physical gag (the hat) starts the motion in frame 0, and the hat becomes the camera's guide, so the viewer wants to see where it lands. The surfacing blocks keep an object arriving every second. The Manhattan slam is the gasp at 13 s. The hat on Manhattan is the laugh that pays off the opening. The return to the windy lookout makes the replay feel like a new gust.
concepts.probe: No Short covers the Nu'uanu slide: "nuuanu landslide" returns only flood clips and a 6.0K "The Megatsunami Nobody's Talking About". "A piece of Hawaii fell into the sea" pulls when it is news: "Hawaii landmark crumbles into Pacific" 1.6M, the Holei Sea Arch collapse at 371K, 245K and 192K. Pali Lookout Shorts get 10-25K ("Can You Handle the Wind?" 10K), so the wind is a known thing. The long-form incumbent is GeologyHub's Nu'uanu slide at 194K. Our edge is a real 3D debris field with a Manhattan overlay and a character thread, in an empty Shorts niche.

concepts.premise: Rank 4 of 12. Ch3 3:30-4:40 (the Big Island stands up, Everest at the same scale, 33,500 ft, the climber vs the summit road). Suggested title: "The Highest Point on Earth Isn't on the Tallest Mountain". A paper climber plants his flag on Everest. Then we drain the ocean around Hawaii and Mauna Kea rises taller from its base, and someone drives up to near its top. The worn "taller than Everest" fact, retold as a rivalry with a punchline.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "This is the highest point on Earth." Frame 0: the Everest summit ridge (SRTM 1", VE 1.0, low oblique) under a blue sky with spindrift. A paper cut-out climber (a real PD mountaineer photo, e.g. US Army 10th Mountain Division via NARA, VERIFY rights) plants a flag on the summit, and the flag is snapping. Label "EVEREST" (Barlow cap 110, y 260).
concepts.payoff: Live drain: Mauna Kea rises out of its full base beside Everest at the same scale. The "33,500 FT" counter rolls as the water falls, and a yellow dashed line at Everest's summit height shows Mauna Kea poking above it. "From the sea floor, Mauna Kea is more than thirty-three thousand feet tall. Taller than Everest." The laugh: a paper 4x4 (a PD vehicle photo) rolls up to the observatory domes and the driver steps out in shorts: "And you can drive almost to the top." Cut back to the climber's drooping flag ("Meanwhile, this guy..."). Spine facts #1 and #3. VERIFY #20 (the summit road). The wording "almost to the top" is already safe. Keep the gag respectful of Mauna Kea.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Put the ocean back, and once again, / this is the highest point on Earth." The refill sinks Mauna Kea back to "just an island". A whip-pan returns to Everest, the climber raises the drooping flag, it snaps in the wind, and the shot lands on the exact frame-0 camera and pose. The line is true both ways: sea level is Everest's home turf. Record it as one take and split at the seam.
concepts.beats:
Text zone: x 60-900, y 170-1500.
0.0-2.5 Hook.
2.5-4.8 "But it's not the tallest mountain." The climber glances off-frame and the camera whips right.
4.8-8.4 "That one's in Hawaii. Most of it is underwater." The Big Island sits at sea level beside Everest at the same scale and looks small.
8.4-14.0 "From the sea floor, Mauna Kea is more than thirty-three thousand feet tall." Drain. The "33,500 FT" counter (Anton cap 270, y 280-560) rolls. The Everest-height dashed line appears.
14.0-15.4 "Taller than Everest." Impact.
15.4-19.0 "And you can drive almost to the top." Crash zoom to the summit domes. The paper 4x4 arrives and the door opens.
19.0-20.6 "Meanwhile, this guy..." Cut to the climber; the flag droops.
20.6-25.5 "Put the ocean back, and once again..." Refill and whip back to Everest, landing on frame 0. Loop at about 25.5 s.
concepts.reuses: The Ch3 3:30-4:30 hero shot of the Big Island standing up during the drain, the SRTM Everest mesh at VE 1.0 at the same scale, the "33,500 FT" big counter, and the 4:30 Everest-climber vs summit-road gag, rebuilt with paper cut-outs. The Ch6 refill. New for the Short: Everest as the opening set, the rivalry framing, and the drooping-flag beat.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: Everyone "knows" Everest, so the second line ("not the tallest") starts an argument in the viewer's head that the drain settles visually by 14 s. The car gag lands just as the fact settles, and the drooping flag gives the climber a comic arc. The loop line flips back to Everest's honour, which invites comments ("so which IS taller?"). It is 25 s, and something new happens every 2-4 s.
concepts.probe: The most proven premise of the set, and the most spent: "Mount Everest is NOT the Tallest Mountain" 17M, "The real tallest mountain..." 15M, "Mount Everest is NOT the tallest mountain in the world" 2.1M, "Why This Mountain is TALLER than Mount Everest" 421K, "Mount Everest vs. Mauna Kea" 376K, plus 255K and 108K. The drive-up angle appears only in travel clips (9-14K, e.g. "Drive To The Top Of Mauna Kea Summit" 9.4K). Our edge: a true-scale live drain on real bathymetry instead of side-by-side bars, a two-character comedy, and a loop. The risk is fatigue with the fact, which is why it ranks 4 and not 1.

concepts.premise: Rank 5 of 12. Ch4 7:30-7:50 (French Frigate Shoals, the 2018 vanished island, the monk seal gag, La Perouse Pinnacle). Suggested title: "A Hurricane Washed Away This Seal's Island". A Hawaiian monk seal dozes on its sand island until a 2018 hurricane washes most of it away. Draining the water shows what the sand was sitting on: a whole sunken volcano, with one last rock left above the sea. Then the island grows back.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Islands out here can wash away in one storm." Frame 0: tight low shot of a paper cut-out Hawaiian monk seal (a real NOAA PD photo) dozing on white sand. Turquoise shallows sit behind it, and a dark storm band creeps in at the top of the frame. Kicker "FRENCH FRIGATE SHOALS" (Barlow cap 80, y 220).
concepts.payoff: Two turns. (1) The gag: the seal plops into the water as the sand streams off, surfaces, and looks left and right at an empty reef. (2) The gasp: the drain shows the reef standing on the shoulders of a huge drowned volcano, with La Perouse Pinnacle lit by the yellow rim: "A whole volcano, sunk out of sight. That rock is the last piece still above the sea." The happy ending: "The island is growing back. More than half of it has returned." Spine fact #10 (most of East Island eroded by Walaka in Oct 2018; about 60% back by 2024). No big number. Light VERIFY: monk seals haul out at French Frigate Shoals (NOAA).
concepts.loop: Read together: "The good news? It's growing back. But remember, / islands out here can wash away in one storm." After the regrowth time-lapse the seal flops back onto the new sand. The camera pushes back into the tight frame-0 shot: the seal dozing, the storm band edging into the top. The tight framing hides the island's outline, so the regrown 2024 shape matches the frame-0 sand exactly. Record it as one take and split at the seam.
concepts.beats:
Text zone: x 60-900, y 170-1500.
0.0-2.8 Hook.
2.8-7.0 "In 2018, a hurricane washed most of this one away." Pull back to the whole East Island (pre-storm outline from imagery). A storm spiral sweeps across, the sand streams off, the outline turns yellow-dashed, and the seal plops in.
7.0-8.6 Gag, no VO: the seal surfaces and looks left and right.
8.6-12.8 "Drain the water, and you see what the sand was sitting on." Drain. The reef platform and the volcano flanks rise.
12.8-19.0 "A whole volcano, sunk out of sight. That rock is the last piece still above the sea." La Perouse Pinnacle gets the yellow rim, label "LAST ROCK" (cap 100).

25.5-27.0 "But remember..." Push back to frame 0. Loop at about 27 s.
concepts.reuses: The Ch4 7:30-7:50 French Frigate Shoals scene: La Perouse Pinnacle ("the last tooth"), the 2018 before/after shoreline built in the engine, "it's half grown back since", and the monk-seal gag. The seal is rebuilt as a paper cut-out of a real NOAA photo. New for the Short: the storm-spiral wipe, the drain under the shoal, and the tight seal framing that hides the outline at the seam.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: A cute animal sits in frame 0 under a threat that is already visible (the storm band), so the viewer stays to see what happens to it. The seal's confused look is the laugh at 7 s. The drain answers a question the viewer did not know to ask (what was the island sitting on?). The regrowth gives a relieved ending, and "But remember" is a soft cliffhanger back into the storm.
concepts.probe: Monk seals are Shorts gold: "Hawaiian Monk Seal (animation)" 4.7M, "How to pet a Hawaiian Monk Seal (Don't)" 1.4M, "Hawaiin monk seals are kinda helpless" 100K. Vanished-island Shorts pull: "Canada Island That Disappeared" 888K, "An Entire Island Just Vanished" 826K, "How Did an Entire Island Vanish? Sandy Island" 651K. East Island itself is barely covered: "The Island that Disappeared Overnight" has 23K. No one has combined a seal character, the real event and a drain reveal.

concepts.premise: Rank 6 of 12. Ch4 5:45-8:00 plus Ch5 8:15 and 9:55 (hotspot candle, time-machine flight, Nihoa, La Perouse, Midway's ring, Kure's Darwin Point). Suggested title: "Every Hawaiian Island Ends Up Like This". It opens on the ending, empty ocean over a drowned volcano, then shows one Hawaiian island's whole life in 30 s: born on fire, carried northwest, worn down, reduced to a ring of coral, and drowned.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Every island in Hawaii ends up like this." Frame 0: the open Pacific at Kure's position, low oblique. The bright water plane is semi-transparent, so the dark flat-topped silhouette of a drowned volcano shows beneath it, and one seabird glides across. Kicker "EVERY HAWAIIAN ISLAND" (Barlow cap 80) over the headline "ENDS LIKE THIS" (Anton cap 150), y 220-470.
concepts.payoff: The life story ends at Midway: the "28 MILLION YEARS" counter (the only number) and a quick drain-and-slice showing the coral cap on the sunken volcano: "By about twenty-eight million years, the volcano has sunk out of sight. Only a ring of coral is left on top." Then the reveal that closes the circle: "Past here, coral can't keep up, and the volcano drowns for good." We are back at frame 0 and now know what we were looking at. Spine facts #8, #9, #10, #11 and #13. "About twenty-eight million" is the pedant wording. No morphing between islands; each real island is shown at its real position.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Past here, coral can't keep up, and the volcano drowns for good. / Every island in Hawaii ends up like this." At Kure the water rises over the reef ring and the ring fades under the surface. The camera settles on the frame-0 composition: the same drowned silhouette under bright water, the same seabird path, the age bar full. On the replay "like this" is no longer a mystery but a verdict. Record it as one take and split at the seam.
concepts.beats:
Text zone: x 60-900, y 170-1500. A slim age bar sits along the top at y about 190, with no digits.
0.0-2.6 Hook.
2.6-5.2 "But it starts here, young and on fire." Whip-pan southeast to the Big Island: glowing lava at the coast, steam.
5.2-9.4 "The sea floor slowly carries it northwest, away from the heat." 3 s cut-away: the plume, and the plate sliding "like paper over a candle" (15 px arrow).
9.4-11.2 "It gets older. Smaller." 1.5 s eased hops to Maui, then Oahu, each filling at least a third of the frame.
11.2-12.6 "Carved into canyons." Kauai.
12.6-15.8 "A sliver of rock that people once farmed." Nihoa, with terrace lines drawn in yellow on the DEM.
15.8-18.2 "The last tooth of a volcano." La Perouse Pinnacle.
18.2-26.5 Midway ring. The "28 MILLION YEARS" counter (Anton cap 230, stacked, y 280-620). Drain-and-slice of the coral cap.
26.5-31.5 Kure. The water closes over the ring and the shot settles on frame 0. Loop at about 32-34 s.
concepts.reuses: The Ch4 5:45 hotspot cut-away (candle under paper), the 6:05-7:00 time-machine flight (Maui, Oahu with the scar, Kaua'i canyons), the 7:00 Nihoa terraces on the DEM, the 7:30 La Perouse Pinnacle, the Ch5 8:15 Midway reef-cap cut-away with the 28 MILLION YEARS counter, and the 9:55 Kure/Darwin Point. New for the Short: it starts at the end, the whip-pan list cadence (look-book S9), and the semi-transparent water showing the drowned silhouette.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: It opens on an ending the viewer cannot read yet, so curiosity carries them through the story. Every 1.5-3 s there is a new island, a new stage of age, and a new shape (lava, green, canyons, sliver, tooth, ring). The number comes late, at 19 s, as the climax. The last line turns the first frame from an empty ocean into a grave, so the replay lands differently. This is the most "satisfying" structure of the set.
concepts.probe: Proven: "Hawaii Is Much Bigger Than You Think - The Secret Hidden Islands" 14M, "How Long Is Hawaii, Really?" 7.4M, "How Do Atolls Form?" 592K, "Northwestern Hawaiian Islands #geography #geology" 118K. The hotspot-conveyor explainers are weak ("Ages of the Hawaiian Islands" 16K, "Hawaii's Secret: What Is a Hotspot Volcano?" 14K, "Hawaii Is the Tip of a Volcano Chain That Reaches Russia" 10K, "Hawaii Is Moving Toward Japan" 2.5K). Our edge: one island aging in a single 3D flight that starts at its own grave, against flat maps and diagrams.

concepts.premise: Rank 7 of 12. Ch5 8:45-9:55 (the battle, the honest wreck geography, three hull silhouettes on the abyssal plain). Suggested title: "Where Are the Ships From the Battle of Midway?" A myth-buster with respect: the carriers are not at Midway. Drain the ocean and draw the line, and they lie far out on the flat ocean floor, about three miles down. Two have never been found. No gags; these are war graves.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Where are the carriers from the Battle of Midway?" Frame 0: Midway Atoll from a low oblique at golden hour, a calm sea, and the reef ring in the lower middle of the frame (above y 1500). Headline "MIDWAY" (Anton cap 150, y 300). Quiet low strings, with no sting.
concepts.payoff: "Not here." A thick yellow line (12 px core with a dark under-stroke) draws from the atoll far out across the drained abyssal plain. Then a vertical plunge down the water column (this format is built for depth) to three simple home-built hull silhouettes, with the "3 MILES DOWN" counter as the only number: "Three have been found, about three miles down. Two have never been found." Two empty dashed markers fade in and out. Spine facts #14 and #15 and must-fix #2: only the three surveyed wrecks, no positions implied for the unfound two, no OET/NOAA imagery, no treasure framing, music down. VERIFY the Akagi depth (it is not in the spine; Kaga is about 5.4 km and Yorktown about 5 km).
concepts.loop: Read together: "They're still out there, somewhere in the dark. So the question still stands: / where are the carriers from the Battle of Midway?" The refill brings the water back. The camera rises up the column, flies back along the yellow line, and settles on the frame-0 golden-hour atoll as the "MIDWAY" headline returns. Because two carriers really are unfound, the closing question is honest, not a trick. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.premise: Rank 8 of 12. Ch6 10:15-10:45 (Kama'ehuakanaloa on the drained south flank, the "COMING SOON" sign gag). Suggested title: "Hawaii Is Building a New Island". A real-estate "COMING SOON" sign pokes out of empty ocean off the Big Island. As the water drains, the camera follows its pole down, and down, and down, to the summit of a young volcano 3,200 ft below. The opening date: thousands of years at least.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Hawaii is building a new island." Frame 0: open ocean off the Big Island's southeast coast, with Kilauea's coastline and steam on the horizon in the top third. A paper "COMING SOON" real-estate sign (Anton lettering cap 120, inside x 60-900) sticks out of the waves, bobbing. Nothing else is in the frame.
concepts.payoff: The visual gag carries the number. The camera rides the sign's pole down as the water drains, and the pole keeps going and going while the "3,200 FT" counter rolls, until it ends on the summit of a young dark cone. "It's a young volcano, and it's active. It could become the next Hawaiian island." Then the sign flips (paper flap) to "OPENING: NOT SOON" over the line "Opening date? Thousands of years, at least." Spine fact #16: "could" and "thousands of years at least" are the pedant wording. The hook's "building" refers to the volcano growing; the body hedges on the island.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Slowly, but surely, / Hawaii is building a new island." The refill rises up the long pole and the camera rides the waterline back to the surface. The sign flips back to "COMING SOON" and the frame settles on the frame-0 composition: the same sign, the same bob phase, the same horizon. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.probe: The premise exists but underperforms: "Hawaii's Next Island Is Already Growing Underwater!" 2.3K, "Lo'ihi: The Newest Hawaiian Island Forms" 4.1K, "This sea is not empty. concepts.premise: Rank 9 of 12. Ch5 8:00-8:15 (the gooney-bird landing gag plus the Midway drain). Suggested title: "This Bird Lands on a Volcano. Badly." A Laysan albatross crash-lands on Midway, faceplant and tumble included. Then we drain the ocean: the sandy island it can't land on is the flat top of a giant drowned volcano, and the bird has no idea. It shakes off and goes around again, which is the loop.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "This bird is about to land on top of a volcano." Frame 0: low oblique over Midway's Sand Island at golden hour. A paper cut-out Laysan albatross (a real USFWS PD photo, wings spread) is on final approach, filling about 40% of the frame height and sliding toward the sand. Label "MIDWAY" (Barlow cap 90, y 240).
concepts.payoff: Two beats. The laugh: on "Badly." the bird flares, faceplants and tumbles (paper flip, sand puff, comic squawk), and a second albatross crash-lands behind it. The gasp: the drain lifts the atoll into the flat top of a huge drowned volcano rising from the dark floor, with the bird a speck in an inset circle: "Midway is the top of a volcano that sank out of sight. The sand is a cap of coral on its summit." "It has no idea." Spine facts #11 and #17. VERIFY #17: the "gooney birds" WWII nickname and the colony wording before the line "In World War Two, the troops here called them gooney birds." No big number.
concepts.loop: Read together: "It shakes it off, goes around, and once again, / this bird is about to land on top of a volcano." After the refill the bird waddles, runs, takes off and circles. The camera follows the arc and lines up behind it for another approach, matching the frame-0 pose, wing angle, light and camera exactly. A failed landing followed by another attempt is a natural loop, so the replay reads as attempt number two. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.premise: Rank 10 of 12. Ch5 8:15-8:45 (Darwin's 1842 guess, the Midway drill, the reef cap on basalt). Suggested title: "Darwin Guessed What's Under This Island. It Took 123 Years to Check." (The number stays in the title only.) A paper Darwin peers into Midway's lagoon, guesses there is a sunken volcano below, and waits so long that cobwebs grow and an albatross nests on his head. Then a drill clanks onto volcanic rock and the Juice Check stamp lands: right.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Darwin never saw what's under this island." Frame 0: Midway's reef ring at low oblique with a bright lagoon. A paper cut-out of Charles Darwin (a real PD photo, older and bearded, with a warm off-white paper edge) leans over the reef edge, peering down into the water. Label "MIDWAY" (Barlow cap 90, y 240).
concepts.payoff: The drill rig (a PD USGS or Navy photo cut-out, VERIFY rights; or a simple rendered derrick) bores through the coral layers in a cut-away and goes CLANK on basalt with a spark. Headline "VOLCANO" (Anton cap 170). The drain then reveals the whole flat-topped volcano under the reef cap, and the Juice Check verdict stamp "DARWIN: RIGHT" slams on (the brand device, used for a verdict as intended). Spine facts #11 and #12. The claim stays at "reefs sit on volcanoes that sank" and never claims Darwin explained the ring shape. Drill: USGS 1965, "more than a century later". No big number on screen.
concepts.loop: Read together: "He was right. Shame, really, because / Darwin never saw what's under this island." The refill brings the water back, the cobwebs blow off, the albatross flaps away, and paper Darwin leans back over the edge into the exact frame-0 pose and camera. On the replay the hook reads as a sad punchline rather than a mystery. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.payoff: The drain joins the four islands. The published maximum-extent outline of Maui Nui draws on in yellow with a 55% orange fill, and the Big Island's outline lifts off, flies over and lands inside it with room to spare. concepts.premise: Rank 12 of 12. Ch1 0:47-1:10 (the 1975 south-coast drop on the 10 m DEM). Suggested title: "Why Are These Palm Trees Standing in the Sea?" A solemn true story with no gags. Palm trees stand in the ocean at dawn. Rewind to before dawn one morning in 1975: the coast lurches toward the sea, drops deeper than a basketball hoop is high, the sea floods in, a tsunami follows, and two people die. By sunrise the beach is gone.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Palm trees, standing in the sea." Frame 0: an early-sunrise close shot on the 10 m DEM of the Big Island's south coast below the Kilauea cliffs. A grove of palms stands in shallow water with small waves washing around the trunks, cliffs behind, and a warm glow on the horizon (luma at least 70). No text: the image is the question.
concepts.payoff: "Before dawn one morning in 1975, this stretch of coast lurched toward the ocean. The ground dropped, deeper than a basketball hoop is high. The sea rushed in. Then came a tsunami. Two people died." There is a silence beat, then "Parts of this shore never came back up." A yellow height bar, not a prop, measures the drop, and there are no numerals on screen. Spine fact #7: the drop is up to 12 ft, so the hoop wording is true. VERIFY #7 (Halape) before any place name, and VERIFY that the submerged-palm image is real (USGS HVO post-1975 photo); if confirmed, show it as a 2.5 s PD full-bleed at 17.6 s. If it cannot be verified, do not make this Short.

The camera eases into the exact frame-0 keyframe: the same palms in the water, the same wave phase, the same sunrise grade. The noun-phrase first line has no tense, so it works both as the hook and as the end of the last sentence. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.premise: Working title: 'We Pulled the Plug on Hawaii'. Someone yanks a giant bath plug next to Hawaii's Big Island. In one continuous live shot the ocean drains away while a vintage paper surfer rides the falling water down. The beach becomes a ledge, the ledge becomes a cliff, and five volcanoes merge into one mountain standing on the sea floor. Then the sea refills and the plug drops back in. Pure watch-it-happen satisfaction with one true payoff: the postcard island is only the tip. Producer rank #2 of 12. If S12 is also picked, S01 must stay on the northeast (Hilo / Mauna Kea) side with the surfer and plug so the two Big Island drains never look alike. Facts: spine #1 and #4. 'Five volcanoes' comes from the brief's 3:30 scene line (standard USGS) but is not in the spine table, so VERIFY the wording.
concepts.hook: First line (Rodney): "This is what's under Hawaii when we pull the plug." (10 words, about 3.9 s; "This is what's under Hawaii" lands by 1.5 s.) First frame, already moving: the Thumbnail-1 camera turned 9:16, a low oblique off Hilo looking southwest. Turquoise sea fills the lower half; the green island and Mauna Kea's summit sit in the top third under pale haze. A giant rubber plug on a chain sits just offshore, and its chain snaps taut on frame 1 as the first swirl forms. A paper-cut vintage surfer (a public-domain Waikiki photo) rides a small wave near the shore. The yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line sits on the real 0 m contour, with a 'SEA LEVEL' plate (Barlow 800, cap 88 px) at x 80-480, y about 700.
concepts.payoff: Around 19-28 s the water is gone. The last water sits in a ring (the real Hawaiian Deep from ETOPO, not sculpted) and '-18,000 FEET' slams onto the gauge. Then the camera, low on the moat floor, tilts up one single mountain with the surfer a speck at its very top: "That surfer was riding the very tip of all this." Then the ocean roars back, and the plug drops into its hole on the last word.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Put the ocean back, and nobody on that beach would ever guess / this is what's under Hawaii when we pull the plug." Last frame = first frame. The refill slows the camera into the opening pose exactly as the water touches the SEA LEVEL line. The surfer rides the last of the rising water back onto the same wave, and the plug seats with a PLUNK. Frame 0 is the identical state with the chain going taut. The water is still on both sides of the cut. The plunk sound runs straight into the chain CLANK. The music bed is cut on a bar so its last bar resolves into bar 1. The voice fragment ends 0.15 s before the cut.
concepts.beats: 0.0-3.9: Plug yanked, whirlpool opens, water starts sliding down the flank while the SEA LEVEL line stays put. VO line 1. | 3.9-7.0: The shore falls away and drowned reef steps break the surface; the surfer drops with the water. VO: "The beach becomes a ledge." | 7.0-10.0: The camera tilts down the flank, following the waterline. A slim depth gauge on the left edge (x 40-110, y 330-1450, no digits) slides down. VO: "The ledge becomes a cliff." | 10.0-13.0: VO: "And the mountain keeps going." | 13.0-18.0: The coastlines vanish and five volcanoes merge into one massif; a yellow rim pulses once. VO: "Five volcanoes turn out to be one mountain." | 18.0-23.5: The water reaches the last ring. Big number '-18,000' (Anton, cap 260 px, yellow) with 'FEET' (Barlow, cap 96) stacked below, inside x 80-880, y 230-560, lands on a gauge thunk. VO: "The last water sits in a ring, eighteen thousand feet down." | 23.5-28.5: A low camera on the moat floor tilts up the whole mountain; the surfer is tiny at the top. VO: "That surfer was riding the very tip of all this." | 28.5-34.0: The refill roars up and the camera rises with it into the opening pose; the surfer rides back onto his wave and the plug drops in. VO: "Put the ocean back, and nobody on that beach would ever guess..." (cut at 34.0). Total 34 s, 66 words. Vertical exaggeration 1.0 for the whole massif (the close reef steps may use up to 1.5). All key text inside x 72-900, y 170-1500 (clear of the right 15% and the bottom 20%).
concepts.reuses: Rebuilt from the cold open (0:00-0:11: the Thumbnail-1 camera, the yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line, the draining water plane), the Ch3 drain from -4,000 m to -5,500 m with the Hawaiian Deep ring (3:30-3:55), and the refill back to the thumbnail frame (11:45-12:30). Also reuses the HMRG 50 m + ETOPO terrain, the depth gauge, and the drain riser, rumble and gurgle sounds. New for the Short only (the long-form is untouched): the plug-and-chain prop (the look book's 'drain plug' map-object gag), the paper surfer cut-out (public-domain photo; rights check per the brief's section 12), and one continuous 9:16 camera path that follows the waterline down instead of the film's cuts.
concepts.why_watched_to_end: The gauge works as a countdown that only bottoms out at 19 s, and the surfer gives the eye one thing to follow all the way down. Once the mountain is revealed, the refill is a reversal people need to see finish. PREMISE: Someone yanks a giant bath plug next to the Big Island. In one continuous vertical shot on the northeast side (Hilo and Mauna Kea), the ocean drains away. A paper surfer gets stranded on his board as the water slides out from under him. The beach becomes a ledge, the ledge becomes a cliff, and the five volcanoes fuse into one mountain standing in its moat. Then the sea roars back and the plug seats. This is the title's own premise ('only the tip') in its purest form, with no Everest and no 56,000.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'This is what's under Hawaii when we pull the plug.' ('what's under Hawaii' lands by 1.5 s.) Frame 0 is the Thumbnail-1 camera turned 9:16: a low oblique about 35 km northeast of Hilo looking southwest, vertical exaggeration (VE) 1.0, sunrise key light from the left. Turquoise sea fills the lower half; the green island and Mauna Kea's summit sit in the top third under pale haze. A giant rubber plug on a chain sits just offshore. Its chain snaps taut on frame 1 (CLANK) and the first swirl forms. The paper surfer (a public-domain Waikiki surf photo cut-out) rides a small wave near the shore. The yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line sits on the real 0 m contour, with its plate (Barlow 800, cap 88) at x 80-480, y about 700.

PAYOFF: The last water pools in the real Hawaiian Deep. It is drawn from ETOPO, never sculpted, and the narration calls it a moat. 'ABOUT / -18,000 / FEET' slams onto the gauge. Then a low camera on the wet moat floor tilts up the whole massif and finds the surfer, a speck marked by a 6 px white zoom ring, still stranded at the very top: 'That surfer was riding the very tip of all this.'

LOOP: Read together: 'Put the ocean back, and nobody on that beach would ever guess / this is what's under Hawaii when we pull the plug.' The refill carries the camera back into the opening pose. The returning wave scoops the surfer back onto his wave. The plug drops in with a PLUNK exactly as the water touches the SEA LEVEL line, so the last frame matches frame 0 (plug seated, chain slack), and frame 0 begins with the chain snapping taut. The PLUNK runs into the CLANK. Cut the music on a bar. The last word ends 0.15 s before the cut. Record VO8 and VO1 as one Rodney take and split it at the seam.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.9: The plug is yanked and a whirlpool opens. The water slides down the reef while the SEA LEVEL line stays put. VO1.
- 3.9-6.2: The water slides out from under the surfer and leaves him standing on his board on the dry reef ledge (paper wobble, a 'boing'). VO: 'The beach becomes a ledge.'
- 6.2-8.4: An eased tilt down the flank, following the waterline. A slim depth gauge sits on the left edge (x 40-110, y 330-1450, no digits). VO: 'The ledge becomes a cliff.'
- 8.4-10.6: Drowned reef terraces flash past as the riser builds. VO: 'And the mountain keeps going.'
- 10.6-15.0: An eased 2 s pull-back to a vertical regional oblique. The coastlines vanish, the volcanoes merge into one massif, and a yellow rim pulses once. VO: 'Five volcanoes turn out to be one mountain.' (VERIFY)
- 15.0-21.0: The water reaches the moat, with a gauge thunk. Number block: kicker ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '-18,000' (Anton cap 260, yellow), FEET (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-880, y 230-560. VO: 'The last water pools in a moat around it, about eighteen thousand feet down.'
- 21.0-26.5: The moat-floor camera tilts up the mountain at VE 1.0 and finds the surfer. VO: 'That surfer was riding the very tip of all this.'
- 26.5-33.0: The refill roars up and the camera rises with the waterline. The surfer is back on his wave and the plug seats. VO: 'Put the ocean back, and nobody on that beach would ever guess...' (cut at 33.0).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500. Every cap height is at least 80 px.

FACTS: Spine #1 (the Mauna Kea side) and #4 (the Hawaiian Deep, about 18,000 ft). VERIFY 'five volcanoes' (USGS lists Kohala, Mauna Kea, Hualalai, Mauna Loa and Kilauea). Fallback line: 'Its volcanoes turn out to be one mountain.' The moat is drawn only where ETOPO shows it.

REUSES: The cold open, 0:00-0:11 (the Thumbnail-1 camera, the SEA LEVEL line, the water plane). The Ch3 drain from -4,000 to -5,500 m with the Hawaiian Deep (3:30-3:55). The refill back to the thumbnail frame (11:45-12:30). Also the HMRG 50 m + ETOPO terrain, the depth gauge, the drain riser, rumble and gurgle sounds, the film's grade, Anton and Barlow, and the yellow accent. New, and only in the Shorts project (the long-form edit stays locked): the plug-and-chain prop, the paper surfer, and the continuous waterline-following 9:16 camera.
seven.why:
It goes first because it is the long-form's own packaging in motion: the same camera and the same yellow SEA LEVEL line as Thumbnail 1. Everyone who watches it is primed to recognise the long-form's card later in Suggested and Browse. It pays off the title ('only the tip') without spending the film's Everest beat or its 56,000-ft climax.

It uses the most proven Shorts format in the probe (drain or flush the ocean: 31M, 23M, 10M, 4.9M), while every Hawaii version that exists is a low-effort upload at 1.2-1.3K views. It beat P2-01 ('every photo is cropped'), which has the same 'only the tip' premise; P2-01's best beat moved into #7.

I fixed one logic hole in S01. The surfer is now stranded on the reef ledge instead of riding the water down, so he really is at the top when the camera finds him. The gauge works as a countdown that bottoms out around 18 s, the surfer gives the eye one thing to follow, and the refill plus the plug on the last word close both open questions in the final second.

Release plan for the set:
- #1 on D0 mirrors the title and thumbnail.
- #2 to #6 follow the film's own order (Ch1, Ch2, Ch4, Ch5, Ch6) on D+1, D+3, D+5, D+7 and D+8/9. A viewer who taps through lands on familiar ground, and the payoff stays hidden.
- #7, the 56,000-ft payoff, runs on D+10 (never before D+7) to re-ignite the film in its second week.

Cut entirely: S03 and P2-12 (1975). They have the weakest proof, a solemn tone, and they depend on two VERIFY items, including whether the key image exists at all.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: You Can't Walk From Maui to Lanai (Unless...). About 25 s, 51 words. The one big number is -400 FEET. Release on D+1.

PREMISE: A paper tourist with a suitcase wants to walk to the next island. We drain about 400 ft of ocean, and Maui, Molokai and Lanai fuse into Maui Nui. He hops across the dry channel past a ferry lying on its side on the seabed. The twist: this is not a what-if. In the last Ice Age they really were one island. Then the sea comes back and he races the tide home.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'You can't walk from Maui to Lanai.' (2.7 s.) Frame 0 is a shore-level vertical oblique from West Maui, looking west across the channel. Lanai sits on the horizon in the top third. Molokai's east end appears at the right edge only if the framing allows; Kaho'olawe stays out of frame. The paper tourist, in a red aloha shirt with a suitcase (a public-domain traveller photo; rights check), stands at the waterline centre-left with his feet at y about 1350. A wave is already washing over his toes. Labels: MAUI near his feet (Barlow 800, cap 90, y no lower than 1450) and LANAI on the horizon island (cap 90).

PAYOFF: The gag comes first: 'No ferry needed', with three paper hops past the beached ferry. Then the real payoff: 'And this isn't a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokai and Lanai really were one island.' This plays over a golden-hour pass across the land bridge as he reaches Lanai and waves.

LOOP: Read together: 'Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, / you can't walk from Maui to Lanai.' During the refill he grabs his suitcase and sprints back ahead of the rising water, while the ferry rights itself and floats. His last hop lands him on his frame-0 mark just as the wave reaches his toes. The camera eases onto the frame-0 keyframe and the -400 block rolls off: same pose, same wave phase. Record VO7 and VO1 as one take and split it at the seam.

BEATS:
- 0.0-2.7: Hook.
- 2.7-5.8: VO: 'Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean.' On 'drain', a gurgle and riser play and the water starts to fall. '-400' (Anton cap 260, yellow) with FEET (Barlow cap 96) rolls in at x 80-700, y 230-560.
- 5.8-7.6: No VO. An eased lift to a vertical regional oblique, with Molokai on top, Maui on the right and Lanai lower left. Tan banks surface and the channels close. A yellow rim draws around Maui, Molokai, Lanai and the Penguin Bank lobe. Kaho'olawe stays separate and dimmed.
- 7.6-9.4: VO: 'Three islands become one.' A MAUI NUI plate lands (Barlow 800 cap 96, x 80-620, y 600-720).
- 9.4-11.0: A crash zoom to the dry channel floor in low golden light. Three squash-and-stretch hops past the paper ferry lying on its side. VO: 'No ferry needed.'
- 11.0-13.0: VO: 'And this isn't a what-if.'
- 13.0-18.5: A golden pass over the land bridge. He reaches Lanai, sets down the suitcase and waves. VO line 6.
- 18.5-25.0: The refill race and the landing on frame 0. VO line 7 (cut at 25.0).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #5 and must-fix #1. VERIFY on the HMRG grid that the saddles surface at about -120 m. Flag: the islands have subsided since the Ice Age (spine #4 gives about 2.5 mm a year for Hawai'i Island), and the Pailolo Channel reaches about 258 m at its deepest (state data; the actual saddle depth must come from the grid), so today's saddles may sit deeper than 400 ft. If the grid needs more, the counter shows the grid's value and VO2 becomes 'Unless we drain a few hundred feet of ocean'. The Ice Age line stays as history. The ferry gag claims nothing (a real Maui-Lanai ferry does run).

REUSES: The Ch1 0:14 Maui Nui drain (the terrain, the yellow rim, Penguin Bank, the dimmed Kaho'olawe), the 0:20 golden-hour pass over the land bridge, and the 0:25 suitcase-tourist gag as a paper cut-out. New, Short only: the shore-level vertical camera, the beached-ferry prop and the race-the-tide refill.
seven.why:
Its payoff is the long-form's 0:14 hero shot. Anyone who taps through from this Short sees what they came for within 20 s of the film, which is the best first Related Video experience we can give.

The premise has real Shorts demand: inter-island travel pulls 5.4M, 181K and 77K, and lost land bridges pull 3.6M, 806K and 187K (Doggerland). Yet 'Maui Nui' has zero geology Shorts.

P2-02's hook beat S02's. It gives a character with a goal and an obstacle in 3 s, using a line everyone knows is true, instead of opening on a number. S02's Maui Nui name and its Ice Age twist were merged in. P2-11 (the crown, '50% bigger') was cut: it reuses the same fusion shot and needs a VERIFY on the reconstructed outline.

At 25 s it is the second-shortest Short. Something moves every 2 s, and the 'will he make it back?' chase resolves only on the loop line.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: Where Did Half of This Volcano Go? About 33 s, 71 words. The one big number is 125 MILES. Release on D+3.

PREMISE: A tourist at Oahu's windy Nu'uanu Pali Lookout loses his hat. We follow it down the cliffs and out to sea, drain the ocean, and find the rest of the Ko'olau volcano lying on the sea floor in giant blocks. One block is bigger than Manhattan, and the hat lands on it. An updraft brings the hat home, and the idiom lands as the punchline.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'About half of this volcano is missing.' (2.7 s; 'half of this volcano' lands by 1.3 s.) Frame 0 is vertical, at the stone railing of the Pali Lookout on the real Ko'olau terrain. A paper tourist (a public-domain photo of a man in a hat; rights check) stands at the railing in the lower-left third. Jagged green cliffs fill the frame behind him and cloud tatters race past. Kicker: PALI LOOKOUT, OAHU (Barlow 800 cap 80, y about 240). On frame 0 the hat is already lifting off his head, with a gust sound.

PAYOFF: A true-size orange Manhattan outline (55% fill, 6 px white outline) drops from the top of the frame and slams onto the largest block, with room to spare: 'One piece is bigger than Manhattan.' A crash zoom finds the tiny hat sitting on it. Then the scale snaps out along a trail of wreckage about 125 miles long, 'one of the largest landslides on Earth.' The final gag payoff: the hat lands back on his head.

LOOP: Read together: 'So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because / about half of this volcano is missing.' During the refill the hat floats up off the block. An updraft carries it back across the sea and up the cliffs, and the camera follows on an eased move into the opening pose. The hat drops onto his head, and that is frame 0, where the next gust lifts it again. The wind whoosh runs straight across the cut. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-2.7: The hat lifts and tumbles over the railing. VO1.
- 2.7-6.2: A 2 s eased dive chases the hat down the cliff face. VO: 'These cliffs on Oahu are where it broke off.' (VERIFY)
- 6.2-10.1: The hat flutters out over the windward sea and the camera rises to a regional oblique northeast of Oahu. VO: 'Long before anyone lived here, it slid into the sea.'
- 10.1-13.5: Drain to about -4,000 m. Blocks surface one by one under a low sun, with a thump about every second, and the depth gauge sits on the left edge. VO: 'Drain the ocean, and it's still lying there.'
- 13.5-17.0: The Manhattan slam (impact_deep sound, dust puff). A MANHATTAN plate lands (Barlow 800 cap 92, x 80-600, y 560-680). Crash zoom to the hat (a soft 'boop'). VO: 'One piece is bigger than Manhattan.'
- 17.0-23.5: A 3 s pull-back along the debris trail, which lights up in hero orange. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '125' (Anton cap 260, yellow), MILES (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 230-560. VO: 'The wreckage runs for about a hundred and twenty-five miles. One of the largest landslides on Earth.'
- 23.5-33.0: The refill, the hat's flight home, and its landing on frame 0. VO: 'So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because...' (cut at 33.0).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #6 (about half of the Ko'olau volcano, about 125 miles, 'one of the largest landslides on Earth', the Manhattan comparison). VERIFY two items:
- (a) The line 'these cliffs are where it broke off' (check with USGS). Fallback: cut VO2 and start VO3 at 2.7 s.
- (b) The block size. USGS words it 'about the same size as Manhattan Island', but the ODP Leg 200 site report gives the Tuscaloosa block as about 30 x 17 km. That is several times Manhattan's roughly 59 km2, so 'bigger than Manhattan', with the overlay showing the spare room, is the likely honest line. The final wording follows the HMRG/GLORIA measurement.
No tsunami talk. The slide's age is not spoken, so the Short keeps one number.

REUSES: The Ch2 Pali Lookout hat gag (1:20-1:40), the drain northeast of Oahu with the blocks surfacing (1:40-2:20), the Manhattan-overlay hero shot (2:20-2:50) and the 125-mile pull-back (2:50-3:10). New, Short only: the cliff-dive camera that follows the hat, the hat on the Manhattan block, and the updraft return.
seven.why:
It is the only Short for Ch2, which starts at 1:20, so a viewer who taps through reaches it in under 90 s.

It has the strongest thread in the set. A physical gag is already moving in frame 0, and the hat then becomes the camera's guide. Viewers watch to see where it lands (on the Manhattan block) and whether he gets it back (the last word).

Manhattan is a US anchor and a slam viewers can feel. The Nu'uanu slide has no Short at all: 'nuuanu landslide' and 'manhattan sized landslide' return nothing on this premise, while Shorts about Hawaiian coast collapses pull 1.6M, 371K and 192K.

The merge: S04's claim opens it, because it is a stronger curiosity gap than P2-03's idiom. P2-03's 'hold on to your hat' is saved for the last line, and P2-03's hat-on-Manhattan beat was added. 'About' is back in the hook so the line is true as spoken.

seven.id: S06-big-islands-future + P2-06-ends-like-this (+ S07 Nihoa as a stage)
seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: Hawaii's Big Island Will End Up Like This. About 34.5 s, 79 words. The one big number is 28 MILLION YEARS. Release on D+5.

PREMISE: Open on Midway's ring of coral and call it the Big Island's future. Then one eased flight northwest along the real chain shows a Hawaiian island's whole life: born on the hot spot, carried off the heat, sinking, carved into canyons, a sliver of rock people once farmed, one last tooth, and finally a ring of coral on a volcano that sank out of sight. That last stage is frame 0.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'Hawaii's Big Island will end up looking like this.' ('Big Island will end up' lands by 1.5 s.) Frame 0: Midway Atoll in true colour from a high vertical oblique. The white-and-turquoise reef ring fills about 70% of the frame height, set in deep blue water, with a 6 px white rim and a slow orbit already moving. For sound-off viewers, the headline THE BIG ISLAND'S FUTURE (Anton cap 110, 4 words) sits at x 80-880, y 230-360.

PAYOFF: Every stage is a real island at its real position; nothing morphs. The destination is the ring we opened on: 'Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight. About twenty-eight million years old.' The number block 'ABOUT / 28 / MILLION YEARS' lands as the orbit picks up its opening path.

LOOP: Read together: 'Every island on this line takes the same trip. Which means / Hawaii's Big Island will end up looking like this.' The final eased move arrives on Midway in the exact opening pose and at the same orbit speed. The headline returns in the last 0.5 s, so the orbit simply continues across the cut. The ocean-swell ambience runs through it. Record VO10 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.5: Orbit on the ring. VO1.
- 3.5-5.0: A whip-pan of 6-8 frames with motion blur, southeast to the Big Island. It is huge, with lava glowing at the coast and a 55% orange fill.
- 5.0-11.0: A 3 s cut-away sliver shows the glowing plume and the plate sliding northwest 'like paper over a candle' (15 px arrow). A slim age bar along the top (y about 210, no digits) starts to fill. VO: 'A hot spot builds a giant volcano. Then the sea floor slides it northwest, off the heat.'
- 11.0-12.6: An eased 1.5 s move until Maui fills the frame. VO: 'It starts to sink.'
- 12.6-14.6: Kaua'i's canyons in raking light. VO: 'Rain carves it into canyons.'
- 14.6-18.5: Nihoa, a sliver of cliff in the swell, with terrace lines drawing on in yellow. VO: 'Then it's a sliver of rock that people once farmed.'
- 18.5-20.1: La Perouse Pinnacle with a yellow rim. VO: 'Then one last tooth.'
- 20.1-28.0: Back to the Midway ring on the orbit path. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '28' (Anton cap 300, yellow), MILLION YEARS (Barlow cap 100), at x 80-860, y 220-600. VO: 'Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight. About twenty-eight million years old.'
- 28.0-34.5: The orbit eases into the opening pose and the age bar fades. VO: 'Every island on this line takes the same trip. Which means...' (cut at 34.5).
Each island fills at least a third of the frame. Every move takes 1.5-2.5 s and is eased. All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #8, #9, #10 and #11, plus #4 for the sinking. 'Will end up looking like this' is the film's own framing (at 9:55: 'So that's the Big Island's future'). VERIFY that the fact-check accepts it as the chain's pattern rather than a guarantee. Fallback hook: 'This is where Hawaii's Big Island is headed.'

REUSES: The Ch3 twist (5:15-5:45), the Ch4 hot-spot cut-away and candle metaphor (5:45-6:05), the TIME MACHINE flight over Maui and Kaua'i (6:05-7:00), the Nihoa terraces on the DEM (7:00), La Perouse (7:30), the Midway ring and its 28-million-year counter (8:00-8:45), and the GEBCO data for the northwest chain. New, Short only: the reversed order (the future comes first), the single vertical flight, and the loop that works by orbit continuity.
seven.why:
It is the long-form's backbone in 35 s: Ch3's twist, all of Ch4 and the start of Ch5. That makes it the Short that advertises the most minutes of the film.

The hidden-chain premise is the second most proven in the probe (14M, 7.4M, 2.3M), yet the life-cycle angle exists only as flat diagrams (16K, 14K, 10K, 1.3K). It has the cleanest loop of the seven, because the destination literally is the first frame, and a new shape arrives every 1.5-3 s.

S06 beat P2-06 because a bright ring is a far more arresting phone frame than open water, and 'Big Island' is concrete. Nihoa (S07) is folded in as one stage, with its human line.

Because this Short owns 'Midway is a ring of coral on a sunken volcano', the albatross and Darwin Shorts (S09, P2-09, P2-10) were cut: they pay off on the same reveal. The seal Shorts (S08, P2-05) were cut for the same reason, since French Frigate Shoals and its 'last rock' are a stage here.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: The Carriers Sunk at Midway Aren't at Midway. About 30 s, 63 words. The one big number is 3 MILES DOWN. Solemn: no gags, music down, treated as war graves. Release on D+7.

PREMISE: A respectful myth-bust. The Battle of Midway is named after the atoll, but drain the Pacific and draw the line, and the three carriers found so far lie far out on the flat ocean floor, about three miles down. Two have never been found. The last line says why: the fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'The carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway.' (3.1 s; 'carriers sunk at Midway' lands by 1.5 s.) Frame 0: a low golden-hour oblique from Midway's outer reef edge, looking northwest to the open sea. The reef and Sand Island sit in the lower foreground, above y 1500. This is deliberately not the top-down ring that #4 uses. A thick yellow line (12 px core, dark under-stroke, head dot) is already drawing from the reef toward the horizon. A MIDWAY plate (Barlow 800 cap 96) sits at x 80-460, y 240-340. A low drone bed plays, with no music sting.

PAYOFF: The camera follows the line's head dot out over the drained abyssal plain. Then it plunges straight down the frame, using the 9:16 frame as a depth gauge, to three simple home-built hull silhouettes, each in an inset zoom circle: 'Far out on the flat ocean floor, three have been found, about three miles down.' Then: 'Two have never been found.'

LOOP: Read together: 'The fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why / the carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway.' The refill rises, and the camera climbs the water column and flies back along the line. The line retracts to the reef edge as the camera settles into the opening pose, and frame 0 is the same pose with the line starting to draw out again. The drone bed runs across the cut. Record VO7 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.1: Hook.
- 3.1-9.4: The public-domain NHHC Yorktown photo, 2.5 s full-bleed with a slow push (VERIFY the credit), then back to the atoll as the drain starts. VO: 'In June 1942, four Japanese carriers and the USS Yorktown went down.'
- 9.4-13.7: The atoll stands up as a coral cap on a drowned volcano, and the camera follows the line out. VO: 'Drain the Pacific, and you'd find them nowhere near the island.'
- 13.7-16.4: The line runs 170-190 miles out. Its length shows the distance, so no number is spoken. VO: 'Far out on the flat ocean floor,'
- 16.4-19.6: The vertical plunge to the three silhouettes. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '3' (Anton cap 280, yellow), MILES DOWN (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 220-560. VO: 'three have been found, about three miles down.'
- 19.6-22.4: Two empty dashed hull outlines appear as an icon in the text area, not on the map, so no positions are implied. VO: 'Two have never been found.'
- 22.4-30.0: The refill and the return along the retracting line. VO: 'The fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why...' (cut at 30.0).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #14 (four Japanese carriers sunk, Yorktown lost). Spine #15: Kaga about 5.4 km down and about 190 mi out; Yorktown about 5 km down and about 172 mi out; Akagi found in 2019; Soryu and Hiryu unfound. Must-fix #2: only the three surveyed wrecks, our own hull silhouettes, never OET, NOAA or Vulcan imagery, and no treasure framing. VERIFY Akagi's depth and position (not in the spine) and the closing line 'the fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea' (standard history, but not in the spine). The decoy story was dropped: about 20 copycat Shorts on it flopped at 130-3,000 views, and its wording is still VERIFY.

REUSES: The Ch5 battle beat (8:45-9:30) and its NHHC Yorktown photo, the honest wreck line with the home-built hull silhouettes (9:30-9:55), and the Midway drain and reef cap (8:15). New, Short only: the reef-edge opening, the camera that follows the head dot, the vertical depth plunge and the line-retract loop.
seven.why:
It is the only Short that sells Ch5's 'battle over a drowned volcano', and it reaches the long-form's biggest adjacent audience: US WWII viewers. Midway Shorts pull 5.7M and 5.1M, 'The Carrier That Sank Twice' 1.5M, and Nat Geo's 'Pacific War Wrecks | Drain the Oceans' (2.47M, long-form) proves the drain-plus-wrecks idea.

The paradox hook is on-brand for Myth Juice and true as worded ('carriers', not 'ships'). The vertical plunge is the best use of the 9:16 frame in the set, and 'two have never been found' is a real open mystery that drives comments.

The merge: P2-07's depth plunge and its unfound-two beat went into S10's myth-bust frame, and S10's decoy beat was cut. This Short beat the seal and albatross Shorts because those would repeat #4's sunken-volcano reveal, while this one covers ground nothing else does.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: The Most Optimistic Sign in Hawaii. About 25 s, 48 words. The one big number is 3,200 FEET. Release on D+8 or D+9.

PREMISE: A paper real-estate sign reading COMING SOON / NEW ISLAND sticks out of the open ocean off the Big Island. As the water drains, the camera rides its pole down, and down, and down, 3,200 ft to the summit of a young volcano that could become the next Hawaiian island. Opening date: thousands of years, at least.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'This is the most optimistic sign in Hawaii.' (3.1 s.) Frame 0: open ocean off the Big Island's southeast coast, with Kilauea's coastline and a steam plume on the horizon in the top third. In the centre, a paper sign on a pole bobs in the waves. The board reads COMING SOON (Anton cap 130) over NEW ISLAND (Anton cap 96), inside x 120-860, y 700-1100. Nothing else is in the frame.

PAYOFF: The pole that never ends is a comic hold that also delivers the number. It finally lands on the summit of a small dark cone (THUNK), and a pull-back shows the baby beside the giant massif. Then: 'Opening date? Thousands of years, at least.' An ISH sticker slaps onto the sign after SOON.

LOOP: Read together: '...Thousands of years, at least. Which means / this is the most optimistic sign in Hawaii.' The refill climbs the pole and the camera rides the waterline back up. A gust peels the ISH sticker away and the sign settles into the frame-0 bob phase: same horizon, same bob. The wave sound is continuous. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.1: Hook.
- 3.1-4.3: VO: 'Follow the pole.' The drain starts with a gurgle, and the camera tilts down and rides the pole below the falling waterline.
- 4.3-9.5: VO: 'Three thousand two hundred feet down,' '3,200' (Anton cap 260, yellow) with FEET (Barlow cap 96) rolls in at x 80-860, y 230-520 while the pole keeps going (a comic hold with a pole creak).
- 9.5-13.0: VO: 'it stands on the summit of a young volcano.' The pole ends, planted in the cone (THUNK).
- 13.0-15.5: An eased 2 s pull-back shows the cone on the Big Island's drained flank, with the massif towering above. Optional caption plate KAMA'EHUAKANALOA (Barlow 800 cap 84, x 80-900, y 600-720), never spoken. VO: 'A baby, next to the giants.'
- 15.5-18.5: VO: 'It could become the next Hawaiian island.'
- 18.5-22.0: VO: 'Opening date?' (beat) 'Thousands of years, at least.' The ISH sticker slaps on with 'least'.
- 22.0-25.5: The refill rises up the pole, the sticker blows off, and the shot returns to frame 0. VO: 'Which means...' (cut at 25.5).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #16: the summit is 975 m (3,200 ft) below sea level, it 'could' become the next island, and it will take 'thousands of years at least'. The narration never says 'erupting' or 'active'. The island claim lives only on our joke sign and is hedged by the VO's 'could'. The name is a caption only, so the voice cannot mangle it.

REUSES: The Ch6 opener (10:15-10:45): the young cone on the drained south flank 3,200 ft down, and the COMING SOON sign gag with 'thousands of years at least'. New, Short only: the sign starts above the water on an absurdly long pole, so the vertical drain becomes a measuring tape; the ISH sticker (from S11); and the bob loop.
seven.why:
It is the only Short for Ch6's newborn-volcano beat and the shortest of the seven. It works as a light palate cleanser between the solemn wrecks Short and the big finale.

The frame-0 image, a sign in the open ocean, asks 'on what?' without any words, and the pole that never ends turns the one number into the joke. The premise is unclaimed (Hawaii-specific versions sit at 2.3K and 4.1K), while island-birth Shorts pull 2.2M and 95K.

P2-08's pole structure beat S11's refill-then-drain-again, which is confusing, and S11's 'already under construction' hook stated the island as certain. S11's ISH sticker was kept as the punchline. The new hook keeps every factual claim under the VO's 'could'.

S05 and P2-04 (the Everest parking gag) lost their place because 'taller than Everest' is spent, and #7 already uses Everest as a stepping stone.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: This Beach Is on a Mountain Almost Twice Everest. About 35 s, 73 words. The one big number is 56,000 FEET. Publish no earlier than D+7 (planned for D+10), with the long-form as its Related Video.

PREMISE: One vertical crane shot travels from a black-sand beach on Mauna Loa's lava down through the draining ocean, past the sea floor, and into the dent the mountain's weight has pressed into the planet. Then it rises back up the whole height while the counter climbs to about 56,000 ft, and Everest, on the same base line, reaches about halfway. It is deliberately the opposite of #1: the southwest side (Mauna Loa) instead of the northeast, a fast drain and a cut-away instead of a slow countdown, and a height claim instead of 'the tip'.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'This beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.' (4.7 s; 'beach is on a mountain' lands by 1.6 s.) Frame 0: a low vertical oblique on a black-sand beach on Mauna Loa's lava. A paper Hawaiian green sea turtle (a public-domain NOAA or USFWS photo) basks in the lower third and surf rolls in. Mauna Loa's broad summit sits at the top under pale haze. The headline ALMOST TWICE EVEREST (Anton cap 120) sits at x 80-880, y 230-380. The crane is already easing downward.

PAYOFF: Everest sinks to the dent's base line, and the camera cranes up the full height while 'ABOUT / 56,000 / FEET' rolls. Everest reaches about halfway: 'Measured from its real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall.'

LOOP: Read together: 'And that turtle has no idea / this beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.' The crane continues up through the refilling ocean and decelerates to a stop in the opening beach pose, and the headline returns. This is a natural hang at zero speed: frame 0 is the same pose with the crane easing down from rest. The surf sound bridges the cut. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-4.7: Hook.
- 4.7-8.6: The camera dips below the waterline as the ocean drains in one fast 2 s whoosh. There is no countdown, so it never repeats #1. A MAUNA LOA plate lands (Barlow 800 cap 92, x 80-560, y 600-720). VO: 'Drain the ocean, and most of Mauna Loa was underwater.' (VERIFY)
- 8.6-11.8: The camera reaches the sea floor. Everest (the SRTM mesh on a pedestal that starts from the same base, VE 1.0) rises beside it, just short. VO: 'From the sea floor, it already beats Everest.' (VERIFY)
- 11.8-13.8: The camera keeps going and the ground slices open. VO: 'But that's not the bottom.'
- 13.8-21.5: The crust and Moho sag into a bowl (schematic, drawn from the USGS flexure description), with a 3 s inset of a paper bowling ball pressing into a mattress. VO: 'It's so heavy, it has pushed the ocean floor down, by miles. Like a bowling ball on a mattress.'
- 21.5-28.5: Everest sinks to the dent's base line and the crane climbs the whole height. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '56,000' (Anton cap 240, yellow), FEET (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 220-540. An EVEREST label (Barlow cap 92) sits at its summit. VO: 'Measured from its real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall.'
- 28.5-35.0: The crane rises through the refilling ocean to the beach. VO: 'And that turtle has no idea...' (cut at 35.0).
VE is 1.0 throughout. All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #2: about 56,000 ft from its true base, the sea floor pushed down by as much as 5 miles, always named Mauna Loa, always 'almost twice'. Spine #3: Everest is 29,032 ft. VERIFY in the USGS 'How high is Mauna Loa?' article behind #2 that more of Mauna Loa lies below sea level than above, and that from the sea floor alone it already tops Everest. Fallback: cut VO3 and hold the Everest pop-up silent. VERIFY that the chosen beach is on Mauna Loa lava (USGS geologic map). Punalu'u is the famous turtle beach, but which volcano's flank it sits on must be confirmed; otherwise use a Ka'u or South Kona beach on Mauna Loa. The turtle is optional; the fallback is S12's sunbather.

REUSES: The Ch3 Everest side-by-side at VE 1.0 (3:55-4:30), the Mauna Loa highlight (4:40-5:15), the Ch6 payoff cut-away with the crust and Moho sag, the bowling-ball metaphor, the 56,000 counter and Everest sunk to the same base (11:10-11:45), and the refill (11:45-12:30). New, Short only: one continuous vertical crane down and back up, the turtle beach on Mauna Loa, and the paper bowling-ball inset.
seven.why:
It is the strongest premise of the 24. It carries the most proven idea on Shorts ('Everest is not the tallest': 17M, 2.1M, 421K) with a number nobody uses (the closest Short to 56,000 ft has 263 views). But it spends the long-form's climax, so it goes last: after the film's first week, to re-ignite it in week 2.

It turns the spent fact into a stepping stone ('it already beats Everest... but that's not the bottom'). That is why it beat S05 and P2-04, which end on the spent fact.

S12 beat P2-01 because 'every photo is cropped' is the same 'only the tip' premise as #1, while 'almost twice Everest' is a distinct, testable height claim. P2-01's 'the sea floor isn't the bottom' beat lives on as VO4.

The 9:16 frame suits one continuous crane down and up, and the turtle keeps the cast distinct from #1's surfer, so the two Big Island Shorts share neither a premise, a device, a side of the island nor a payoff.

result.title: You Can't Walk From Maui to Lānaʻi (Unless...)
result.narration:
TEXT SENT TO TTS (ONE request, so the loop seam is one natural take). Voice "Rodney - Clear Educator" (voice_id eY2VJs4Gi8QKG2RV01sS), model eleven_v4, same voice settings as the long-form, with the pronunciation dictionary "MJ-Hawaii" attached. The text is rotated so that VO7 runs straight into VO1:

Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, you can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi. Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean. Three islands become one. No ferry needed. And this isn't a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi really were one island.

51 words, about 20.0 s at 153 wpm.

- Cut the take inside the pause after "ever since,".
- Everything from "you can't walk..." goes to 0.05 s, so the Short opens on at most 0.05 s of room tone.
- "Then the ice melted ... ever since," goes to 20.30-24.60. The rest of that pause (about 0.4 s) fills 24.60-25.00.
- The other lines are placed only by trimming silence between sentences. No time-stretching.

  - VO1 0.05-2.40

  - VO3 7.70-9.05

  - VO7 20.30-24.60

- Lānaʻi -> alias "Lah-NAH-ee". Hawaiian [laːˈnaʔi], with a light glottal catch before the final "ee". Never "luh-NYE".
- Molokaʻi -> alias "Moh-loh-KAH-ee". Hawaiian [moloˈkaʔi]. Never "moh-loh-KYE".

result.hook:
0.0 s, VO: "You can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi." (7 words, 2.35 s).

Frame 0 is already moving. A paper tourist in a red aloha shirt stands at the West Maui waterline with his suitcase, leaning toward the sea. A wave is washing over his shoes. Lānaʻi lies across the horizon under a pinned LĀNAʻI postcard, and a ferry bobs right there.

The image asks the question before the line does: why is this guy about to walk into the ocean? The line answers it with a truism that sounds too obvious to say. That makes the viewer wait for the catch, and the catch comes at 2.75 s ("Unless...").

No greeting, no channel name, no number before 3.2 s.

Probe (ytsearch, 2026-11-08):
- "walk from maui to lanai": the best Short has 12K views and is off-topic. The premise is unclaimed.
- The "You could once walk from England to France" Shorts sit at 0.4-8.9K. That template is weak, and our hook inverts it into a present-tense dare.
- The audience exists. "Why Hawaii's Islands Aren't Connected by Boats" has 5.4M views as a Short, and RealLifeLore's ferry video has 7.07M. "No ferry needed" speaks directly to that crowd.
result.payoff:
The payoff is built in three steps, then a button.

1. GAG (9.4-10.7). "No ferry needed." He makes three squash-and-stretch hops over the stranded ferry, which lies on its side on the dry shelf and lets out one weak, sad toot.

2. TWIST (11.15-12.45). "And this isn't a what-if." The IT HAPPENED verdict stamp slams over the golden pass.

3. REVEAL (13.10-18.10). "In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi really were one island." He reaches Lānaʻi, sets the suitcase down and waves. The camera cranes up into a high golden oblique that shows the three islands joined. The rim re-traces the coast, and LAST ICE AGE / ONE ISLAND lands on "one island".

4. BUTTON, in the last 4.7 s. The sea comes back, and he races the tide home. The closing line, "Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since,", runs into the opening line. "You can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi" stops being a dumb truism and becomes the result of the Ice Age ending. That rewrite of the first line is the real payoff, and it lands exactly on the seam as the wave washes over his shoes.

The Short never spends the long-form's payoff: no 56,000 ft, no dent, no Everest.
result.loop_check:
AUDIO, the last line followed by the first line as one passage:
"Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, you can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi."
- It is plain English with no gimmick: a "since"-clause completed by a main clause. On a first view the opening line still stands alone as a full statement.
- Both halves come from ONE TTS take (the text is rotated so that VO7 precedes VO1), and the cut sits inside the natural comma pause. Prosody, room tone and breath are therefore continuous across the seam.
- The music cue is 96 BPM, 10 bars = 25.000 s, built so that bar 10's pickup leads into bar 1.
- The surf bed is a loop.
- There are no fades in or out.
- Export: video exactly 750 frames and audio exactly 25.000 s. Trim the AAC encoder priming and confirm with ffprobe. Then play the file looped for 3 cycles on a phone and check for any hitch.

PICTURE:
- 24.0-25.0 is not a match-cut. It is the opening shot's own pre-roll: Shot A is rendered as ONE continuous take from t = -1.0 to 5.6, and its first second (-1.0 to 0.0) is placed at 24.0-25.0.
- So the last frame (749) and frame 0 are consecutive frames of the same render:
  - same camera transform and push velocity (the G2 orbit hands off onto that path at the same speed by 24.0);
