  - same 2.5 s idle-sway phase and ferry-bob phase (both are locked to the clip clock: 10 cycles in 25 s);
  - same wave phase (the swash reaches his shoes exactly at the seam);

Spine refers to the ep02 brief's fact spine (section 4). GMRT refers to my check on the Short #2 grid: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/s02_grid/mauinui.asc (about 60 m cells) and wide.asc, run with s02_scripts/saddles2.py and wide.py plus my s02w_scripts/pailolo.py and bridge.py.

1. "You can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi." TRUE. The shallowest crossing between them sits about 50 m (166 ft) down on GMRT, and the State of Hawaii data book gives the channel 77 m maximum. Spine #5 context.

2. "Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean." TRUE. At -122 m (spine #5: Ice Age sea level about -120 m, "roughly 400 ft"; conversions table -120 m = about 400 ft) the Maui-Lānaʻi saddle (-50 m) is dry.
- A pedant may note that about 170 ft already suffices. Our line states a sufficient amount, not the minimum. That is fine, and a likely comment hook.

3. "Three islands become one." TRUE at -400 ft (spine #5; must-fix #1).
- GMRT saddles: Maui-Lānaʻi -50 m (-166 ft); Lānaʻi-Molokaʻi -78 m (-257 ft); Maui-Kahoʻolawe -159 m (-523 ft). So exactly Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi join, and Kahoʻolawe stays separate.
- MUST-FIX #1 VERIFY: closed on GMRT. Re-run saddles2.py on the brief's named HMRG 50 m grid before lock (the margin is 44 m, so no change is expected).
- SUBSIDENCE FLAG: closed. Today's saddles (-50 m, -78 m) sit well above -122 m, so the "-400 FEET" counter and VO2 stand as written. The "a few hundred feet" fallback is not needed.
- PAILOLO: the direct West Maui-East Molokaʻi saddle is -242 m (-792 ft) on GMRT, and the mid-channel water stays connected to the open ocean. So the Pailolo stays an inlet in every drained shot, and Molokaʻi joins through Lānaʻi. This matches USGS Volcano Watch: "A permanent embayment separated East Molokaʻi from West Maui by about 700,000 years ago." The spine's 258 m figure is that channel's maximum depth; it does not block the join.
- PENGUIN BANK lobe inside the rim: spine #5 ("a now-drowned part of the same island"). On the wide grid the merged component reaches lon -157.76 by -100 m.
- KAHOʻOLAWE dimmed and outside the rim: spine #5 and must-fix #1.

4. "No ferry needed." A joke that claims nothing. A real Maui-Lānaʻi passenger ferry runs (brief flag). The company is never named and the paper ferry carries no livery.

5. "And this isn't a what-if." plus the IT HAPPENED stamp. Supported by claim 6.

6. "In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi really were one island." Spine #5: "joined most recently about 18,000 years ago".
- USGS Volcano Watch, "Once a big island, Maui County now four small islands": "Maui, Lanaʻi, and Molokaʻi were connected intermittently thereafter, most recently about 18,000 years ago."
- Grigg et al. 2002 (Coral Reefs, "Drowned reefs and antecedent karst topography, Auʻau Channel"): at the last glacial maximum, Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi were interconnected by limestone bridges.
- On screen as LAST ICE AGE / ONE ISLAND and MAUI NUI (the name is from spine #5).

7. "Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, ..." Spine #5 (Ice Age sea level about -120 m).
- Grigg et al. 2002: about 120 m of sea-level rise in the Holocene transgression flooded these bridges.
- USGS: "Molokaʻi became isolated, and then the land bridging Lanaʻi and Maui was submerged."
- Melting ice raising the sea is standard science and adds no new number.

8. Visual-only details come from data, not invention. The turquoise pools left in the Maui-Lānaʻi floor at -122 m are real basins on GMRT: a straight Olowalu-Mānele profile dips to -136 m, which matches Grigg's solution basins. Show reef pinnacles only where the grid resolves them.

One big number only: -400 FEET. There is no other number on screen or in the VO. The 18,000-year date and the 150,000-200,000-year Kahoʻolawe split stay in the description and pinned comment.

STILL OPEN (VERIFY before lock):
(a) HMRG 50 m re-run of the saddles.
(b) Public-domain rights for the tourist photo (carried over from the long-form's 0:25 cut-out) and for the ferry photo.
(c) Lexicon check on wehewehe.org, plus a full phone-speaker listen.
(d) Confirm that the Barlow Condensed and Anton builds contain U+02BB (ʻokina) and the macron Ā. If not, build the glyph; never drop it.
(e) Confirm the shore camera location is outside the August 2023 Lahaina burn area on the county map.

TITLE: You Can't Walk From Maui to Lānaʻi (Unless...)
- 46 characters.
- Passes the niche regex. It contains none of drained/drain, hidden/hiding, bottom/beneath, nobody or found, and no Everest.
- Backup: "Maui to Lānaʻi on Foot? It Used to Work." (40)

DESCRIPTION:
In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi were one island. Lower today's ocean by about 400 feet and they join up again. Kahoʻolawe stays separate: its land link to Maui broke much earlier.

The full film follows the drained ocean all the way down, to the true base of the mountain under Hawaiʻi:
Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down)

Every depth in this Short comes from real seafloor survey data.
Bathymetry: GMRT (Global Multi-Resolution Topography, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory); University of Hawaiʻi SOEST HMRG multibeam synthesis; NOAA ETOPO 2022.
Sources: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Volcano Watch, "Once a big island, Maui County now four small islands"; Grigg, R.W. et al. (2002), "Drowned reefs and antecedent karst topography, Auʻau Channel, SE Hawaiian Islands", Coral Reefs.
Photos: [public-domain credits for the tourist and ferry photos, filled in after the rights check].

result.narration:
TTS STRING (one ElevenLabs request, "Rodney - Clear Educator", eleven_v4, speed 1.0, sent in story order, 71 words):

Watch the surfer. Sorry, buddy. The beach becomes a ledge. The ledge becomes a cliff. The cliff becomes a mountain. And it keeps going. The last water pools in a moat at its base. About eighteen thousand feet down. Now look all the way back up. And our surfer? Still up there, waiting for a wave. Fine. Put the ocean back. And he has no idea — this is what's under Hawaiʻi.

PLACEMENT (use the word timings): split the last sentence in the pause after "idea". The second half, "this is what's under Hawaiʻi.", opens the Short at 0.12 s. "And he has no idea" ends at 32.85 s, 0.15 s before the cut. The Short plays in this order:
- 0.12 this is what's under Hawaiʻi.
- 2.05 Watch the surfer.
- 3.95 Sorry, buddy.
- 5.05 The beach becomes a ledge.
- 7.00 The ledge becomes a cliff.
- 9.00 The cliff becomes a mountain.
- 11.30 And it keeps going.
- 13.10 The last water pools in a moat at its base.
- 16.75 About eighteen thousand feet down.
- 19.95 Now look all the way back up.
- 22.65 And our surfer? Still up there, waiting for a wave.
- 27.40 Fine. Put the ocean back.
- 31.35-32.85 And he has no idea

Timing rules:
- Total speech is about 24 s. If the take runs past 24.5 s, regenerate the whole request at speed 1.05. Do not cut words.
- Trim the seam pause so that "idea" to "this" spans 0.27 s across the loop.

DELIVERY: calm and dry. Deadpan on "Sorry, buddy." and "Fine." A small lift on "mountain". Slower and lower on "eighteen thousand feet down".

PRONUNCIATION:
- The only spoken Hawaiian word is Hawaiʻi: huh-WHY-ee, with a light glottal catch (the ʻokina) before the final "ee", stress on WHY. Never huh-WHY-yee.
- Send it with the ʻokina (U+02BB). If the take drops the catch or puts a pause inside the word, regenerate. Last resort: a pronunciation-dictionary alias Hawaiʻi -> "Huh-why-ee".
- Hawaiian words that appear only in the description or production notes (never voiced here): Hilo HEE-loh; Honoliʻi hoh-noh-LEE-ee (catch before the last ee); Mauna Kea MOW-nah KAY-ah; Mauna Loa MOW-nah LOH-ah; Waikīkī why-kee-KEE; Kohala koh-HAH-lah; Hualālai hoo-ah-LAH-lie; Kīlauea kee-lau-AY-ah.
- Confirm each on wehewehe.org before any of them is ever voiced.

result.hook:
Frame 0 is already moving. We are low on the water off Hilo, 12 m behind a paper surfer riding a small turquoise wave. Mauna Kea's summit sits in the top third under sunrise haze. Behind him, bolted to the black shore boulders, is a 10 m chrome bathtub overflow plate, with a giant chrome ball chain draped from it into the sea. A bath fixture on a Hawaiian beach is the visual question.

Frame 1 (0.03 s): CLANK. The chain rips taut out of the water toward open sea, a distant THOOMP follows, and the ocean starts sliding out from under the surfer.

The VO starts at 0.12 s: "this is what's under Hawaiʻi." That is 5 words, finished by 1.9 s, and it opens two questions at once: what is down there, and what happens to the surfer. "Watch the surfer." (2.05 s) pins the second question one second before the first gag lands at 3.45 s (BOING, stranded on dry reef, "Sorry, buddy.").

There is no greeting, no channel name and no on-screen text in the first 6 s. Frame 0 and the CLANK carry it with the sound off.
result.payoff:
The number lands first (16.5-19.8). The plug drops back into its plughole with a PLUNK, the whirl stops, and the last water sits in the real Hawaiian Deep as a turquoise pool at the foot of the flank. ABOUT / 18,000 / FEET DOWN slams in over the dark basalt.

Then the payoff (19.95-26.0). "Now look all the way back up." tilts the camera from the plugged pool up the whole flank to the old shoreline at the very top of the frame. A white ring pops on a speck there (22.1), and a loupe opens on it (22.4). It is the surfer, still frozen in riding stance on his board on dry reef. "And our surfer? Still up there, waiting for a wave." One frame now holds the scale: a whole mountain of dark rock between the pool and one speck at the top.

The joke then turns. "Fine. Put the ocean back." (27.4) The sea roars back up the flank and across the shelf as a smooth rising sheet. The camera flies home with it and the water delivers his wave (31.6). The irony line lands in the last 1.6 s: "And he has no idea". The opening line completes it.

Nothing about why the moat exists, Everest, or 56,000 ft is spent. "Why is there a moat?" is left open for the long-form.

"idea" ends at 32.85, the cut is at 33.00, and "this" starts at 0.12, so the pause across the seam is 0.27 s.

result.facts:
CLAIMS (all inside the spine; no number beyond the one big number):
- "this is what's under Hawaiʻi" / the flank shown. Spine #1 (Mauna Kea rises 4,205 m above sea level and about 6,000 m below; USGS FAQ). The terrain is real: UH SOEST HMRG 50 m blended into NOAA ETOPO 2022, plus the NCEI Hilo coastal DEM near shore, at VE 1.0.
- "The beach becomes a ledge." No number. Describes the data on the camera line: ETOPO 15" shows a shelf from 0 to about -400 m that runs ~20 km out from Honoliʻi (-97 m at 5.5 km, -620 m at 20 km).
- "The ledge becomes a cliff." Plain-language word for the shelf break, as the brief's own Ch1 line does ("The shelves end in cliffs"). ETOPO 15" slopes reach 21 degrees over 1 km on the camera line and 31 degrees on the 45-degree line. Production check: on HMRG 50 m, confirm the face on the 60-degree line reaches 30 degrees or more locally. If it does not, the word still stands as colloquial; do not add a number.
- "The cliff becomes a mountain." / "And it keeps going." Spine #1 (about 6,000 m below sea level; more than 33,000 ft from the sea floor). The 33,500 figure is NOT spoken.
- "The last water pools in a moat at its base." Spine #4 (Hawaiian Deep, a moat-like flexural trough; Wikipedia, Hawaiian Trough). My ETOPO 15" check at -5,486 m: the only water left in frame is one connected pool along the island's NE base, about 9,000 km² (155.54-154.09 W, 19.05-21.2 N), deepest -5,764 m. The moat is drawn only from these cells, never sculpted. "At its base" was chosen over "around it" because, from this side, the water lies along the foot of the island rather than visibly ringing it.
- "About eighteen thousand feet down." and on screen ABOUT / 18,000 / FEET DOWN. Spine #4 and the brief's unit table (5,500 m = about 18,000 ft). The pool surface is set at exactly -5,486 m (18,000 ft). "ABOUT" is kept.
- Surfer gag: no claim. Line-of-sight checked on ETOPO: from the payoff camera (+250 m, 66 km out) the surfer spot and Mauna Kea's summit are both in view.

CHANGES FROM THE CONCEPT, AND WHY:
1. Cut "Five volcanoes turn out to be one mountain" (it was marked VERIFY). Kohala, Mauna Kea, Hualālai, Mauna Loa and Kīlauea are already joined as one island above sea level, so a drain cannot reveal them "becoming" one mountain. The line would mislead. The VERIFY and the fallback go with it.
2. Replaced the moat-floor tilt-up camera. On ETOPO, every camera below about -300 m loses the surfer behind the shelf edge, and on the moat floor even Mauna Kea's summit is hidden. The concept's payoff shot is therefore impossible at true scale. From the moat floor the whole flank is also only about a 9-degree band (a ramp, not a tower). The camera instead holds the old sea-surface height and looks down. That keeps every line of sight honest and echoes the long-form title "(Look Down)".
3. Cut the yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line and its plate (clone kit, per the 2026-11-08 update). It is replaced by an in-world salt-white bathtub ring on the real 0 m line and by the overflow plate.
4. Dropped the minus sign: "-18,000" at cap 260 measures 862 px and does not fit x 80-880. "18,000" measures 768 px and fits, and FEET DOWN carries the sign.

NOT SAID (held back for the long-form and Short #7): why the moat exists (the weight and the dent), Everest, 56,000 ft, 33,500 ft.

VERIFY (production, not claims):
- Rights for the surfer photo: public domain only, an anonymous person, never Duke Kahanamoku or any named surfer.
- All Hawaiian pronunciations on wehewehe.org.

result.description_and_link:
TITLE: We Pulled the Plug on Hawaiʻi (29 characters). It avoids drain, hidden, bottom, beneath, nobody and found. An exact-title probe found no match. The premise is proven: "I Accidentally Pulled the Plug on the Ocean" has 10M views, and no Hawaiʻi version exists.

DESCRIPTION (exact):
Pull the plug on the ocean next to Hawaiʻi's Big Island and the coast off Hilo turns into a ledge, a cliff, then a mountain standing in a moat about 18,000 feet deep.
Why is there a moat around Hawaiʻi at all? Full film: Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down) [long-form link]
Real seafloor data at true vertical scale: University of Hawaiʻi SOEST multibeam synthesis and NOAA ETOPO 2022. The plug is not real. The moat is.
#BigIsland #ocean #geography

(The long-form title is quoted exactly as it is published.)

LINK SETUP:
- Publish the long-form first on launch day (D0).
- Publish this Short 10-30 minutes later, in the same hour.
- In YouTube Studio, set the Short's Related Video to the long-form.
- Paste the long-form URL in line 2.

The Short shows the moat but never explains it. The long-form's payoff (the weight denting the sea floor) answers the question in line 2, so the Related Video link is the natural next tap.

PINNED COMMENT: "Have you ever paddled out off Hilo? Would you still, knowing this is under you?"

result.narration:
ON-SCREEN ORDER (72 words, about 28.2 s of speech in 33.0 s). Voice: Rodney - Clear Educator, voice_id eY2VJs4Gi8QKG2RV01sS, model eleven_v4, about 153 wpm.
About half of this volcano is missing. The missing half used to stand right out there. Long before anyone lived on Oʻahu, it slid into the sea. Drain the ocean, and there it is. In pieces. One piece is bigger than Manhattan. The wreckage runs about a hundred and twenty-five miles. One of the largest landslides on Earth. So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because...

EXACT TTS STRINGS. Two takes, same voice settings and seed.
TAKE A (the body, used 2.85-24.6 s):
"The missing half used to stand right out there. Long before anyone lived on Oʻahu, it slid into the sea. Drain the ocean, and there it is. In pieces. One piece is bigger than Manhattan. The wreckage runs about a hundred and twenty-five miles. One of the largest landslides on Earth."
TAKE B (the loop seam, recorded as ONE take, as the brief requires):
"So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because... about half of this volcano is missing."
- Split TAKE B at the zero crossing in its pause after "because...".
- The tail ("So if ... because...") plays at 27.75-32.4 s.
- The head ("about half of this volcano is missing.") plays at 0.05-2.55 s, so the seam is a single performance.
- If that head sounds like a mid-sentence continuation and not a confident cold open, re-roll TAKE B. Do not splice in a separate opener.

EDIT-ONLY PAUSES (inserted from the word timestamps, not typed into the TTS):
- 0.30 s between "Drain the ocean," and "and there it is."
- 0.95 s between "and there it is." and "In pieces."
- 0.6 s between "miles." and "One of the largest...".
- If TAKE B's natural pause after "because..." is shorter than 0.6 s, pad it with room tone to 0.6 s. The hat-landing "pat" sits inside that pause.

PRONUNCIATION. Oʻahu is the only Hawaiian word Rodney says.
- Oʻahu: oh-AH-hoo, IPA [oˈʔahu]. Three syllables, stress on AH, a light glottal catch before AH. Never "oh-WAH-hoo". It is sent to TTS with the real ʻokina (U+02BB).
- Accept a take that gives [oh-AH-hoo] with or without a light catch. If it inserts a full pause or says "oh-WAH-hoo", add a pronunciation-dictionary alias (Oʻahu -> "oh-AH-hoo") and re-render.
- Check it against wehewehe.org, and against a Hawaiian speaker if possible.

Lexicon for Hawaiian words that appear anywhere in this Short's package but are NOT spoken:
- PALI (on screen): PAH-lee
- Nuʻuanu (description): noo-oo-AH-noo [nuˈʔuanu]
- Koʻolau (description): koh-oh-LAU, with "lau" rhyming with "cow" [koˈʔolau]
- Hawaiʻi (description): hah-WAI-ee (or hah-VAI-ee), with a catch before the final ee [haˈvaiʔi]
- Kāneʻohe (production notes): KAH-neh-OH-heh
- Lanihuli (production notes): lah-nee-HOO-lee
- Kauaʻi (not spoken or labelled): kow-AH-ee
- Molokaʻi (not spoken or labelled): moh-loh-KAH-ee

result.hook:
FRAME 0 is a vertical holiday snapshot at the Pali Lookout, already moving.
- The recurring paper tourist stands at the stone parapet in the lower-left third, smiling at the camera.
- The Lanihuli pali wall soars behind him and cloud tatters race over the crest.
- Kāneʻohe Bay and the open sea lie far below.
- His paper hat is already lifting off his head in a gust, brim flapping, and the camera is pushing in.
- Kicker: PALI LOOKOUT / OʻAHU (Barlow 800, cap 84).

VO at 0.05 s: "About half of this volcano is missing." That is 7 words, with "half of this volcano" landing by about 1.3 s.

Why it works:
- The viewer sees green cliffs, not a volcano, and is told half of it is gone. That opens two questions at once: what volcano, and where did half of it go?
- In the same second, the hat gives the eye something to chase over the rail, and the camera follows it straight toward the answer.
- There is no greeting, no channel name and no number before 10 s.
- The premise is unclaimed: probes of "half of this volcano is missing", "oahu volcano collapsed half", "nuuanu slide manhattan" and "tuscaloosa seamount" found no Short on this story.
- Pali Lookout wind Shorts (7-11K views each) show that the place itself is relatable.
result.payoff:
The payoff lands in two stages.

1. THE REVEAL (14.75-24.6 s). Drained, the missing half is still lying on the sea floor in pieces.
   - A true-size orange Manhattan drops from the top of the frame and slams onto the biggest block, lengthwise, with lots of room to spare: "One piece is bigger than Manhattan."
   - A crash zoom finds the tiny paper hat sitting on that block (the "boop").
   - A 3 s pull-back draws the whole wreckage on in orange from Oʻahu's coast to the toe while ABOUT 125 MILES rolls in: "The wreckage runs about a hundred and twenty-five miles. One of the largest landslides on Earth."
   - Each step tops the last: a block, then a city, then 125 miles, then "on Earth".

2. THE GAG PAYOFF, in the last 5 s (28-33 s).
   - The sea refills and the hat bobs up.
   - The trade wind carries it home and up the cliff.
   - It flutters down and settles back on his head just as Rodney says "hold on to your hat, because..."
   - The idiom lands literally, and the unfinished sentence completes itself in the opening line, so the replay starts as the punchline.

LAST LINE INTO FIRST LINE, as one passage:
"So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because... about half of this volcano is missing."

This is natural English. "Hold on to your hat, because..." is the standard idiom for "brace yourself for a surprise", and here it is also literal: the wind has just stolen his hat.
- It is recorded as one ElevenLabs take (TAKE B) and split in the pause after "because".
- The intonation across the cut is therefore one performance.
- The pause is 0.6 s: 32.4 to 33.0 plus 0.05 s of head. The hat-landing "pat" (32.8) sits inside it.

LAST FRAME AGAINST FIRST FRAME:
Frame 989 (32.967 s) and frame 0 are generated by the same deterministic shot function of t mod 33.0, so 989 to 0 is one continuous step of motion, not a match cut.
- Camera: the same camera C0 on the same push-in line. Frame 989 is 2 cm behind frame 0 (0.6 m/s at 30 fps), with zero tilt in both.
- Tourist: the same pose, arm down and card upright.
- Hat: seated and lifting in the new gust, 0.5 cm up at frame 989 and 1 cm up at frame 0.
- Clouds and foliage: the cloud tatters and foliage sway use noise that repeats every 33.0 s.
- Kicker: PALI LOOKOUT / OʻAHU at full opacity in both frames, in the same position.

The cloud-wipe camera change happens at 30.5-30.85 s, well before the seam.

AUDIO:

- The wind bed and music are rendered as a wrapped mix with a 0.5 s crossfade.
- The music is 16 bars at 116.4 bpm, which is exactly 33.0 s, and bar 16 resolves into bar 1, so there is no click or level jump.

result.facts:
Each claim with its source.

1. "About half of this volcano is missing." (this volcano = Koʻolau, which the Pali Lookout sits on)
   - Spine #6: about half of the Koʻolau volcano collapsed.
   - Wikipedia, Nuʻuanu Slide: "The eastern half of the mountain collapsed."
   - USGS Volcano Watch, "Oahu, Niihau and Kauai": "The caldera was bisected by the catastrophic collapse of the Nu'uanu landslide."
   - Status: VERIFIED.

2. "The missing half used to stand right out there." (spoken while the camera looks NE from the lookout)
   - ODP Leg 200 Initial Reports, ch. 1: the landslide "broke away from the northeast flank of Koolau Volcano".
   - The Pali Lookout faces NE over the windward side.
   - Status: VERIFIED.
   - VERIFY item (a) FAILED, so this line replaces the concept's "These cliffs on Oʻahu are where it broke off." Wikipedia says the ridge "appears to be a steep and weathered fault scarp", but "evidence suggests the geographic features are from wind and water rather than the landslide event". Neither the USGS Volcano Watch page nor the ODP report makes a headwall claim.
   - FLAG for the long-form team (no change made by this Short): the long-form's planned Ch2 line "If you've stood here, you've stood on the edge of a break" (1:20) has the same problem.

3. "Long before anyone lived on Oʻahu, it slid into the sea."
   - Spine #6: "more than a million years ago". ODP Leg 200 dates it to 1.8-2.4 Ma (2.1-1.8 Ma per Herrero-Bervera et al. 2002). Wikipedia gives 1-1.5 Ma.
   - Human settlement of the islands was about AD 1000 (spine #9 era).
   - The claim is true under every estimate, and no age is spoken, so the Short keeps one number.
   - Status: VERIFIED.

4. "Drain the ocean, and there it is. In pieces."
   - USGS Volcano Watch: the slide "deposited numerous blocks on the sea floor as far as 100 miles northeast of the island."
   - The drain is framed as a thought experiment ("Drain the ocean").
   - Status: VERIFIED.

5. "One piece is bigger than Manhattan."
   - Spine #6 has the Manhattan comparison.
   - ODP Leg 200 Initial Reports, ch. 1: Tuscaloosa Seamount "is ~30 km long, 17 km wide, and at least 2 km tall". Wikipedia gives the same 30 x 17 km and a summit 2,756 m below sea level.
   - Manhattan is about 21.6 x 3.7 km, with about 59 km2 (22.8 sq mi) of land.
   - So the block is longer, about 4.5 times wider, and about 400 km2 in area (roughly 7 times Manhattan).
   - USGS words it more conservatively ("about the same size as Manhattan Island"). "Bigger" is the conservative reading of the measured dimensions.
   - Status: wording VERIFIED (item b closed).
   - Production check: measure the block's base outline on the HMRG grid before placing the true-size overlay; expect about 30 x 17 km. If the grid disagrees, the fallback line is "One piece is the size of Manhattan." It has the same timing.

6. "The wreckage runs about a hundred and twenty-five miles." (on screen: ABOUT 125 MILES, the Short's one big number)
   - Spine #6: about 200 km (125 mi).
   - Wikipedia: "200 kilometers (124 mi) in length".
   - ODP: it "extends more than 200 km from the island".
   - USGS I-2809: debris carried "as far as 200 km".
   - Status: VERIFIED.

7. "One of the largest landslides on Earth."
   - Spine #6, quoting Wikipedia.
   - USGS "Giant Hawaiian landslides": "ranking them among the largest on Earth".
   - Status: VERIFIED.

8. "So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat"
   - This is an idiom and a joke, not a factual claim. The lookout's wind is well known, and no wind speed is stated.

VISUAL HONESTY:
- The Manhattan outline is true size (US Census TIGER) and sits on the real Tuscaloosa block at its real position (about 22.07 N, 157.08 W).
- The footprint is digitized from USGS I-2809. VERIFY that the sheet's outline layer is legible enough to trace; otherwise use the Moore et al. 1989 USGS figure.
- VE is 1.0 everywhere.
- The ghost of the missing half is a schematic: the surviving western shield flank mirrored and smoothed. It is translucent, never labelled, and described as "a sketch, not a measurement" in the description.
- The hat stays at true scale (tracked by the ring) except in the macro shot. Its flight is obviously a gag.
- There is no tsunami talk or imagery (no wave ring), no Everest, and nothing about the 56,000 ft payoff.

RELEASE: D+3 (three days after the long-form).
- In YouTube Studio, set the Short's Related Video to the long-form "Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down)". That link is the funnel; links in Shorts comments are not clickable.

TITLE: Where Did Half of This Volcano Go?
- 34 characters, a question.
- It contains none of drained/drain, hidden/hiding, bottom/beneath, nobody or found, and no Everest.
- It passes the niche title regex.
- Exact-title probe: 0 on-topic matches.

DESCRIPTION (paste as is):
About half of the Koʻolau volcano, the one that built eastern Oʻahu, broke away more than a million years ago and slid into the Pacific. It is called the Nuʻuanu landslide. Drain the ocean northeast of the island and the pieces are still there. The biggest, Tuscaloosa Seamount, is about 30 km (19 mi) long and 17 km (11 mi) wide: bigger than Manhattan. The whole debris field runs about 200 km (125 miles), one of the largest landslides on Earth.

The full story of what's under Hawaiʻi: Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down)

Every depth in this Short is real survey data. The pale outline of the missing half is a sketch, not a measurement.
Seafloor: University of Hawaiʻi SOEST HMRG multibeam synthesis; NOAA ETOPO 2022. Oʻahu terrain: USGS 3DEP. Manhattan outline: U.S. Census TIGER.
Sources: USGS Volcano Watch, "Oahu, Niihau and Kauai"; ODP Leg 200 Initial Reports, Chapter 1 (Nuuanu Landslide); Moore et al., "Prodigious submarine landslides on the Hawaiian Ridge" (USGS); Moore et al., "Giant Hawaiian landslides" (USGS); USGS Geologic Investigations Series I-2809, "Hawaii's Volcanoes Revealed" (Eakins et al. 2003).

result.title: Hawaii's Big Island in 28 Million Years
result.narration: Hawaiʻi's Big Island will look like this. A hot spot builds a giant volcano. Then the sea floor slides it northwest, off the heat. Slowly, it sinks. Rain carves it into canyons. Then it's a sliver of rock that people once farmed. Then one last tooth. Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight. About twenty-eight million years old. Every island on this line takes the same trip. Which means Hawaiʻi's Big Island will look like this.

Spoken and shown claims, each with its brief fact-spine line or a VERIFY tag:

1. VO1 / headline, "Hawaiʻi's Big Island will look like this" / "THE BIG ISLAND'S FUTURE":
   - This is the chain's pattern: #8 (the Pacific plate carries the volcanoes northwest; the chain gets older to the northwest), #11 (Midway is a shield volcano that sank while its reef grew upward) and #13 (past Kure, islands drown).
   - It matches the film's own framing at 9:55 ("So that's the Big Island's future").
   - VERIFY: the fact-check must accept it as the chain's pattern, not a guarantee. If not, use the fallback hook "This is where Hawaiʻi's Big Island is headed."
   - "End up" was dropped on purpose: the true end state is a drowned seamount (#13).
2. "A hot spot builds a giant volcano." #8 (hotspot origin of the chain). The Big Island sits over the hot spot (#8, #16).
3. "Then the sea floor slides it northwest, off the heat." #8 (the Pacific plate moves northwest over a fixed hotspot). The rate (5-10 cm a year) is not spoken.
4. "Slowly, it sinks." (shown over Maui)
   - #4: Hawaiʻi Island subsides about 2.5 mm a year.
   - #5: Penguin Bank is a now-drowned part of Maui Nui.
   - #11 and #13: the older volcanoes sank.
   - Maui itself: USGS Volcano Watch "How high was Haleakalā?" gives East Maui subsiding about 0.3 mm a year now and about 2.1 mm a year averaged over the past million years.
   - VERIFY: add the Maui line to the fact ledger.
5. "Rain carves it into canyons." (Kauaʻi)
   - This is the brief's Ch4 wording ("older still: carved into canyons"), but it is not a numbered spine fact. VERIFY.
   - Support: Waimea Canyon was cut by the Waimea River, fed by heavy rain from the island's centre, along the edge of an old volcanic collapse (Wikipedia, Waimea Canyon State Park).
6. "Then it's a sliver of rock that people once farmed." #9 (Nihoa: Native Hawaiians around AD 1000; farm terraces, house sites and platforms).
   - The terrace positions drawn on screen must come from a published Nihoa site map (the same source as the long-form at 7:00). VERIFY.
7. "Then one last tooth." #10 (La Perouse Pinnacle, about 37 m: the last volcanic rock of French Frigate Shoals).

8. "Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight." #11 (a shield volcano that sank while its reef grew upward; 1965 USGS drilling) and #12 (atolls are reefs on sunken volcanoes).
   - The ring-shape mechanism is not claimed.

result.description_and_link:
DESCRIPTION, pasted as-is:

Hawaiʻi's Big Island is riding the Pacific plate northwest, away from the hot spot that built it. Fly up the island chain and every island is a later stage of the same trip: Maui, Kauaʻi, Nihoa, La Perouse Pinnacle at French Frigate Shoals, and finally Midway, a ring of coral on a volcano about 28 million years old.

Most of every Hawaiian island is out of sight. The full film looks down: Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down)

Every island in this Short is real and in its real place, and heights are not exaggerated. The cut-away under the Big Island is a diagram, not to scale. Nihoa, French Frigate Shoals and Midway lie in Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument.

Sources:
- USGS, How big are Hawaiian volcanoes?
- USGS Volcano Watch, How high was Haleakalā?
- Dalrymple, Clague and Lanphere (1977), Revised age for Midway volcano, Hawaiian volcanic chain
- USGS Midway Atoll drilling (1965)
- Hawaii hotspot, Nihoa, French Frigate Shoals, Midway Atoll and Waimea Canyon (Wikipedia)

EXACT TTS INPUT (one ElevenLabs call, voice "Rodney - Clear Educator", voice_id eY2VJs4Gi8QKG2RV01sS, model eleven_v4; solemn read: stability about 0.6, style 0, speed 1.0):

"In June, nineteen forty-two, four Japanese carriers and the U.S.S. Yorktown went down. Drain the Pacific, and you'd find them nowhere near the island. Far out on the flat ocean floor, three have been found, about three miles down. Two have never been found. The fleets never saw each other. They fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why the carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway."

HOW THE TAKE IS CUT (this makes the loop): cut the take in the natural gap (about 80-150 ms) between "why" and "the". Piece B, "the carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway.", plays at 0.00 as the hook. Piece A, from "In June" to "That's why", plays from 3.25 s, so that "why" ends at 29.92. Because the hook and the closing line come from one sentence in one take, the replay sounds like one continuous sentence. Listen to the hook on its own too. The answer, in three parts:

1. Distance, shown and not spoken (9.4-13.7). The camera climbs to a high oblique. The line runs straight up the vertical frame, from Midway's drowned volcano to a dot 189 miles out, at Kaga's recorded position.

2. Depth (13.7-19.6). The camera swoops down to the old sea-surface height and falls straight down with a yellow plumb, until the whole 9:16 frame is the depth gauge.
- The number block lands with sonar ping 2: ABOUT / 3 / MILES DOWN. This is the Short's only big number.

3. The count and the reason (19.6-29.92).
- The five paper discs from 5.5 s return: three solid, two dashed and empty. "Two have never been found." A third sonar ping goes out and gets no echo.
- The sea closes back over the grave.
- The final 4.5 s give the reason, which the hook only asserted: "The fleets never saw each other. They fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why..."

CLAIM-BY-CLAIM AGAINST THE BRIEF'S FACT SPINE (brief section 4)

1. "The carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway." Spine #15 plus must-fix #2. The wrecks lie on the abyssal plain, not on the atoll: Kaga about 306 km (190 mi) out, Yorktown about 277 km (172 mi) out.

2. "In June, nineteen forty-two," Spine #14 (Battle of Midway, 4-7 June 1942).

3. "four Japanese carriers ... went down." Spine #14.

4. "and the U.S.S. Yorktown went down." Spine #14 (Yorktown lost). It sank on 7 June 1942 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Yorktown_(CV-5)).

5. "Drain the Pacific, and you'd find them nowhere near the island." Spine #15 plus must-fix #2 (170-190 miles out). Framed as a thought experiment ("Drain...").

6. "Far out on the flat ocean floor," Spine #15 ("They lie on the abyssal plain, not on the atoll").

7. "three have been found," Spine #15: Yorktown found May 1998, Kaga Oct 2019, Akagi 2019. Only these three.

8. "about three miles down." Spine #15 plus the brief's conversion table (5.4 km is 3.4 mi, "about 3 miles down").
- Kaga: about 5.4 km.
- Yorktown: about 5 km (16,650 ft), which is 3.15 mi.
- Akagi was VERIFY and is now checked: 18,011 ft (5,490 m), about 3.4 mi (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_aircraft_carrier_Akagi; the Battle of Midway article says "nearly 18,010 ft (5,490 m)"). Add it to the ledger.

9. "Two have never been found." Spine #15 (Sōryū and Hiryū unfound).
- Re-checked 2026-11-08: no report of either being located.
- NHHC says time ran out in 2019 "before we could mount an extensive search for the other two Japanese carriers, Soryu and Hiryu" (https://usnhistory.navylive.dodlive.mil/Obituaries/Article-View/Article/2686990).
- Re-check the news on upload day (D+7).

10. "The fleets never saw each other." VERIFY (not in the spine).
- Support from search: NHHC, "Battle of Midway, 3-6 June 1942, Combat Narrative", says the surface ships in both forces never see each other and all attacks are by air (https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/b/battle-of-midway-3-6-june-1942-combat-narrative.html). The page returned 503 today, so read it directly before lock.
- Britannica's Midway explainer says the two surface fleets never sighted each other (https://www.britannica.com/video/219024/context-location-Battle-of-Midway-World-War-II).
- Never say "first": Coral Sea came first.
- If it fails, use the 63-word fallback.

11. "They fought with planes, from far out at sea." VERIFY (not in the spine; standard history).
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway: "Land-based planes from Midway and carrier-based planes from the U.S. fleet surprised and attacked Nagumo's force." Spruance launched "at extreme range".
- Caveat: the line describes how the fleets fought, not what sank each ship. A submarine finished Yorktown, and Japanese destroyers scuttled the burning Japanese carriers.

12. "That's why the carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway." This follows from 6 and 11, with no new claim.

VISUAL FACTS
- The line ends at Kaga's recorded sinking position, 30°23′N 179°17′W (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_aircraft_carrier_Kaga). By haversine from Sand Island that is 304 km (189 mi) at bearing 323°, which matches spine #15's 190 mi.
- The three found wrecks do not lie in one direction:
  - Akagi sank at 30°30′N 178°40′W: 176 mi at 334°, about 38 mi from Kaga.
  - Yorktown, per its infobox coordinates (30°35′59″N 176°34′4″W): 172 mi at 016°.
- So only the Kaga hull is drawn on the map, at the end of our line. Akagi and Yorktown are counted only in the off-map disc row. This follows must-fix #2: no fake positions. That is why there are not three inset circles at one plunge point.
- Hulls sit upright: Kaga "sits upright", Akagi "upright, on its keel", Yorktown "sitting upright" (the Wikipedia articles above). The silhouettes are drawn upright.
- Hull and plane silhouettes are home-built, generic and unmarked. No OET, NOAA or Vulcan imagery, no flags, no gore, no treasure framing (must-fix #2).
- War-grave framing: NHHC Director Cox calls them "important war graves of both American and Japanese sailors" (https://nautiluslive.org/blog/2023/09/14/exploring-iconic-shipwrecks-battle-midway-provide-never-seen-details).
- The four-plus-one disc grouping follows spine #14. Found/unfound by disc: Kaga, Akagi and Yorktown solid; Sōryū and Hiryū dashed (spine #15).
- Midway's cream crown on a dark drowned volcano follows spines #11 and #12. The cap band is schematic: limestone above about -400 m, using the spine's 157 m and 384 m drill figures.
- The plunge depth is real ETOPO/GEBCO depth at Kaga's position. Sample it first; expect about 5.4 km.
- The planes approach Midway from the northwest. That matches the Japanese air strike on Midway on 4 June (Battle of Midway article), but it stays an illustration: unmarked, with no narration about who they are.
- VERIFY the NHHC Yorktown photo's catalogue number and public-domain status. It is the same file the long-form uses at 8:45-9:30.

Dropped: the "AF is short of water" decoy (still VERIFY, and its copies flopped). No Everest, no Hawaiian place names in the narration, no on-screen sources.

DESCRIPTION (no emojis, sources only here):
The Battle of Midway is named for the atoll, but the carriers sunk in it lie far out on the open Pacific floor, about three miles down. Kaga, Akagi and USS Yorktown have been found. Sōryū and Hiryū never have. The wrecks are war graves of Japanese and American sailors, inside Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument.

Watch the full film, with the ocean around Hawaiʻi drained away: Why Can't You See Most of Hawaii? (Look Down). It is linked above.

Approximate depths and distances: Kaga about 5.4 km (17,700 ft) down, about 190 miles from Midway; Akagi about 5.5 km (18,000 ft) down; Yorktown about 5.1 km (16,650 ft) down, about 172 miles from Midway. Seafloor from GEBCO and NOAA ETOPO 2022. The ship and plane shapes are our own simple drawings, not images of the wrecks.

- Naval History and Heritage Command, Battle of Midway, 3-6 June 1942, Combat Narrative
- Ocean Exploration Trust, Nautilus Live, "Exploring Iconic Shipwrecks of the Battle of Midway" (Sept 2023)
- Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, Kaga discovery (Oct 2019)
- MIT News, Yorktown found (June 1998)
- Wikipedia: Battle of Midway; Japanese aircraft carrier Kaga; Japanese aircraft carrier Akagi; USS Yorktown (CV-5)

PINNED COMMENT (a place with living memory): "Did someone in your family serve at Midway, on either side? Tell us their story." Heart and answer family stories. No jokes in replies.

result.narration:
TTS REQUEST, sent as one text in one take. Voice: Rodney - Clear Educator (eY2VJs4Gi8QKG2RV01sS), model eleven_v4, the long-form's voice settings. Generate 2-3 takes. Keep the take whose "Which means" ends open and rising and whose "this is" starts clean.

"Follow the pole. Keep going. Three thousand two hundred feet down, it stands on the summit of a young volcano. A baby, next to the giants. It could become the next Hawaiian island. Opening date? Thousands of years, at least. Which means this is the most optimistic sign in Hawaiʻi."

PLAYBACK ORDER IN THE SHORT. Cut the take in the silent gap between "means" and "this", at a zero crossing with 5-8 ms fades. The take's last sentence becomes the opening hook at 0.03 s. "Which means" closes the Short at 24.10-24.80 s.

"This is the most optimistic sign in Hawaiʻi. / Follow the pole. / Keep going. / Three thousand two hundred feet down, / it stands on the summit of a young volcano. / A baby, next to the giants. / It could become the next Hawaiian island. / Opening date? / Thousands of years, at least. / Which means..."

Length: 50 words and 71 syllables, about 19.5 s of speech inside 25.0 s. The gaps are the comic beats.

Delivery: deadpan on "Keep going." and "Opening date?" Leave a natural 0.5 s pause after "Opening date?"; the edit places it. The number is written in words so the voice says "three thousand two hundred", not "thirty-two hundred".

PRONUNCIATION NOTES FOR RODNEY (every Hawaiian word in this Short)
- Hawaiʻi (spoken, in the hook and loop line). Target: hah-WHY-ee, with a light glottal catch before the final "ee" (IPA həˈwaɪʔi). Acceptable fallback: plain English huh-WHY-ee. Never huh-WAH-yuh or huh-WAH-ee. The TTS text carries the real ʻokina (U+02BB). If a take swallows or garbles the last syllable, add a pronunciation-dictionary alias "Hawaiʻi" -> "Hah-why-ee". Aliases work on every model; phoneme tags may not work on eleven_v4.
- Hawaiian (spoken; an English adjective, correctly written without the ʻokina). Say huh-WHY-un, never huh-WAH-yun.
- Kamaʻehuakanaloa (on screen only, never spoken). KAH-mah-ʔEH-hoo-ah-kah-nah-LOH-ah, with a glottal stop before EH and the main stress on LOH. The parts are kama 'child', ʻehu 'reddish', a 'of', Kanaloa. If it is ever voiced, use the alias "Kah-mah-eh-hoo-ah-kah-nah-loh-ah", and check it on wehewehe.org, ideally with a Hawaiian speaker, before rendering.
- Description-only names, for the channel lexicon:
  - Kīlauea: kee-lau-EH-ah
  - Lōʻihi: LOH-ʔee-hee
  - Kanaloa: kah-nah-LOH-ah

result.loop_check:
LAST LINE INTO THE FIRST LINE, as one passage:
"...Opening date? Thousands of years, at least. Which means this is the most optimistic sign in Hawaiʻi. Follow the pole..."

This reads as one natural English sentence. "Which means" (24.10-24.80, open and rising) flows straight into "this is the most optimistic sign in Hawaiʻi" (0.03). Both come from the same TTS take, so the seam is the take's own 0.2 s gap between "means" and "this". It is cut at a zero crossing with 5-8 ms fades. A first-time viewer hears a clean statement; a replay viewer hears the conclusion of the joke.

LAST FRAME vs FIRST FRAME
- The last frame (749, at 24.967 s) uses the same camera as frame 0: K0, 5 m from the pole, eye 0.6 m above the water, heading 343°, pitch -3°, vertical fov 30°.
- The state matches:
  - water back at 0 by 24.00, and splash spray gone by 24.50;
  - the -ISH sticker out of frame by 24.45;
  - board sway at phase 0 (a 2.5 s period, 10 whole cycles);
  - a wave field built only from periods that divide 25.0 s, so the waves are in the same phase;
  - static clouds and identical light;
  - the same captions as the opening (WHICH MEANS... hands over to THIS IS THE).
- From 24.50 to 24.967 the picture is the frame-0 state in motion. That meets the playbook's last 0.5 s rule.

SOUND
- The wave bed is one seamless 25.0 s loop, crossfaded tail into head.
- Music is 10 bars at 96 bpm (2.5 s per bar = one sway); bar 10 resolves into bar 1.
- The settle's slap and creak at 24.9 meets the slap and creak at 0.0.

QC GATE
- First/last-frame MAE must be about 5/255 or less.
- Concatenate the Short with itself and run temporal_scan.py: no 'cut' or 'flash' may appear at the join.
result.facts:
1. "Three thousand two hundred feet down" and the counter 3,200 FEET.
- Spine #16: summit 975 m (3,200 ft) below sea level.
- Source: USGS HVO Volcano Watch, 27 Jan 2022, "Kamaʻehuakanaloa - the volcano formerly known as Lōʻihi Seamount": "rising to 3,189 ft (975 m) below sea level".
- 3,200 is the brief's own rounding (unit table: -975 m = 3,200 ft). The description says "about 3,200 feet (975 m)".
- Render note: the ETOPO 2022 hero grid smooths the summit to -1,023 m at 18.922N 155.263W, so the counter is keyed to the grid summit.

2. "it stands on the summit of a young volcano."
- Spine #16, same USGS page: "the youngest volcano in the long line of the Hawaiian-Emperor chain."
- "It" is our prop pole; the pole stands at the DEM summit.

3. "A baby, next to the giants."
- A metaphor, located by spine #16. USGS, same page: "19 miles (30 km) south of the Kīlauea coastline."
- The giants are the Big Island's volcanoes. Not spoken: Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth (ledger C3-10).

4. "It could become the next Hawaiian island."
- Spine #16: "Say it 'could' become the next island."
- USGS, same page, describes its eventual emergence "forming a new island", far in the future.
- The NEW ISLAND claim lives only on the joke sign and is hedged by "could".

5. "Opening date? Thousands of years, at least."
- Spine #16, USGS: "It will be millennia before Kamaʻehuakanaloa emerges."
- Brief must-fix 4, pedant wording: "thousands of years at least".

6. "This is the most optimistic sign in Hawaiʻi."
- A joke about our own prop; it makes no factual claim.

7. On-screen name KAMAʻEHUAKANALOA.
- Spine #16 (renamed in 2021, formerly Lōʻihi).
- USGS: "in July 2021, Lōʻihi Seamount was renamed Kamaʻehuakanaloa by the Hawaii Board on Geographic Names."
- It is a caption only, never voiced.

8. Visual: at a sea level about 3,200 ft lower, the summit breaks the surface as a small crescent islet.
- From the DEM (ETOPO 2022 / Terrain Tiles hero grid): at -1,100 m the summit rim shows as two islets.
- The same DEM shows a submarine bench about 24 km north at about -1,000 m that also surfaces. The render team must re-run sill.py / flood-fill on the production grid before locking the frame.
- VE is 1.0 in every shot, so no "heights exaggerated" line is needed.

9. Description lines.
- The name meaning, "reddish child of Kanaloa": USGS Volcano Watch 2022, quoting Kuʻulei Kanahele of the Edith Kanakaʻole Foundation.
- "Youngest volcano in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain", "about 19 miles off Kīlauea's coast" and "millennia": all from the same USGS page.

Never said: erupting, active, 1996, or any eruption date. There is no on-screen source.

VERIFY: none open in the narration or on screen.

This sign stands on a 3,200-foot pole. At the bottom is the summit of Kamaʻehuakanaloa, the youngest volcano in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain, about 19 miles off Kīlauea's coast on Hawaiʻi Island.

result.swipe_risk_0_2s:
MODERATE-HIGH. Here is what the thumb sees in the first 2 s: a photoreal beach, a paper tourist with a suitcase, a pinned LĀNAʻI postcard, a bobbing ferry, surf and a ukulele pluck. That reads as a Maui travel Short. The packaging blind test already found the postcard device reads as "travel video" (13 skips). The VO "You can't walk from Maui to Lānaʻi." (0.05-2.40) is a truism, and it ends on a name half the audience cannot place, so on its own it creates no tension. The turn ("Unless...") lands at 2.75 s and the first anomaly (the sea pulling out) at 3.2 s. Both come after the swipe decision. The draft says "The image asks the question before the line does: why is this guy about to walk into the ocean?" That does not hold on a phone. A 6-degree lean is invisible at 390 px, and a tourist standing at the waterline is normal tourist behaviour, not a question.

Fixes that keep the loop intact:
(1) Let the frame-0 backwash simply keep going. The swash still hits his shoes at frame 0, then from about 1.2-1.5 s it pulls back too far, too fast, with the bathtub gurgle starting under it. The drain then begins inside the window.
(2) Close the 0.35 s VO gap so "Unless" lands at 2.2 s or earlier.
(3) Give him a readable intent at frame 0: one foot lifted to step into the sea, suitcase swung forward. Mirror it at 23.8-24.0 so frame 749 still equals frame 0.
(4) Do not open bar 1 on a pure ukulele/surf travel-vlog bed. Get the gurgle or a wrong note into the mix by 1.5 s.
result.mid_drop_risks:
1) 5.40-7.70: a 2.3 s VO hole across the lift and Shot B. The merge happens at 6.6 and 6.9 with only clicks, before anyone has told the viewer what to watch. Molokaʻi has never been named or labelled at that point (it is first said at 14.45). An unlabelled regional map changing shape reads as "map stuff", so this is the most likely early drop. Fix: put the (rewritten) VO3 on the clicks, e.g. "Lānaʻi snaps onto Maui. Molokaʻi snaps onto Lānaʻi.", with one paper slip per name landing on each island.

2) 13.10-18.10: the weakest stretch. A 5-second sentence carries three Hawaiian names in a row ("In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi really were one island.") over a slow crane. The crane re-shows merged land the viewer already saw at 7.5, and "ONE ISLAND" repeats "Three islands become one" from 7.7. A repeated reveal at 55-70% of the runtime is the classic Shorts dip. It also fails the place-match gate: Maui and Lānaʻi are named at about 14.45-16.45 with neither label on screen (MAUI left at 5.9 and LĀNAʻI at 3.1; both return only at 23.5-23.85). Fix: compress it to 3.5 s or less, drop a slip per name as each is said, and add a real twist here (see payoff).

3) 18.10-20.30: a second 2.2 s VO hole plus "The music cuts dead on the beat (18.75), leaving only the rumble". The double-take carries part of it, but dead air plus a rumble reads as disaster, not comedy (see must-fix). Keep the hole at 1.2 s or less and comic.

4) 23.0-24.0: six events land in about 0.5 s (landing, clock roll-off, flip, card flutter-in, MAUI pop, orbit hand-off). Illegible at phone size. It is harmless because it resolves into frame 0, but moving the card's return to about 22.9-23.4 would let each event read.

5) Production risk: everything hangs on Shot A. A shore-level camera 2.2 m up needs a near-field swash shader and a 1-3 m lidar tile. That is the hardest untested asset in the whole look book (U6 terrain is "not yet good enough"), and the loop depends on it rendering as one continuous take. If it looks like a game, frames 0-30 lose the swipe test. Pick a fallback camera before building the rest (e.g. a 150-300 m low oblique over the same beach, same push, same props).

6) The good beat to protect is 9.4-10.7: the hops over the stranded ferry and the "sad toot". It is the best retention moment in the draft.
result.payoff_strength:
MODERATE, about 6/10.

The strongest visual moment comes early, at 6.6-8.1 (the clicks, -400 landing, the rim). After that the Short keeps confirming what it already showed. The stated payoff, "Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi really were one island", is the "you could once walk from X to Y" template. The draft's own probe calls that template weak in Shorts (0.4-8.9K). My probe agrees: the best "ice age land bridge" Short has 67K. "Our hook inverts it" changes the hook, not the payoff.

The loop rewrite of line 1 ("ever since, you can't walk...") is clever but subtle. Most viewers will not consciously register it. It helps replays more than it satisfies. The race home is the most fun beat and gives the end energy.

Upgrade, true and cheap: turn the IT HAPPENED stamp into a twist. Add "Nobody ever walked it, though. People hadn't reached Hawaiʻi yet." (new ledger line, VERIFY: Polynesian settlement about AD 1000-1200; spine #9 already dates Nihoa to about AD 1000.) This gives a real "huh". It heads off the certain "there were no humans then" comment. It also makes the tourist the first person ever to try, which makes the race funnier. It flows into the seam: "...People hadn't reached Hawaiʻi yet. Then the ice melted..."

Alternative twist, unique to our data but better saved for another Short: you still could not walk straight from Maui to Molokaʻi. The direct Pailolo saddle is -241.5 m on GMRT, so you would have to go through Lānaʻi.

What the grid confirms:
- West Maui-Lānaʻi join between -50 and -55 m. Molokaʻi joins between -78 and -82 m. Kahoʻolawe stays separate all the way to -122 m.
- The direct Pailolo saddle is -241.5 m, and mid-Pailolo water stays connected to the open ocean, so the inlet is correct.
- "Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean" is right as a sufficient amount, not a minimum.
- "really were one island" matches C12-05 (USGS: "most recently about 18,000 years ago"; the link was intermittent and Kahoʻolawe is excluded).

Problems:
(1) Implication. IT HAPPENED slams down over a man walking the bridge, but no human was in Hawaiʻi then (settlement was about 1,000 years ago). That is a pedant magnet. Add the "nobody walked it" line, or put the stamp on the map without the walker.
(2) Honesty of the process, plus sensitivity. The refill ("a deep rumble: foam fronts race in", "The water roar rises", and him fleeing) shows a rise that took thousands of years as a sudden surge. On a West Maui beach it reads as a tsunami. That clashes with the brief rule "No mega-tsunami hype", with Hawaiʻi's 1946 and 1960 history, and with Lahaina's 2023 sensitivity.
(3) Fact #8 is wrong. "A straight Olowalu-Mānele profile dips to -136 m, which matches Grigg's solution basins" does not hold: the -128 to -139 m cells near 20.761N 156.809W are connected to the open ocean at -122 m, so that hollow is an inlet, not a basin. (4) Race geography. The 265-degree route is dry at -122 m: its deepest point is -80 m from Launiupoko and -116 m from Olowalu. result.title: This Beach Is on a Mountain Almost Twice Everest
result.narration:
TTS INPUT. Send this verbatim as ONE generation (Rodney - Clear Educator, eleven_v4, about 153 wpm). Make 3 takes and keep the take where "this beach..." sounds strongest as an opener:

It's Mauna Loa, and most of it is underwater. From the sea floor, it already beats Everest. But that's not the bottom. It's so heavy it pushed the sea floor down, by miles. Like a bowling ball on a mattress. Measured from its true base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall. And that turtle has no idea this beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.

PLAYBACK ORDER. Split the last sentence in the silence between "idea" and "this". Its tail, "this beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.", plays at 0.00 s as VO1. Sentences 1-6 play from 4.90 s to about 26.6 s as VO2-VO7. "And that turtle has no idea" plays from 29.85 to 32.20 s as VO8. The loop seam is therefore one continuous take, and the hook and the body come from the same voice pass.

As heard (71 words, 27.8 s of speech in a 32.4 s Short):
VO1 This beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest. (12 words)
VO2 It's Mauna Loa, and most of it is underwater. (9)
VO3 From the sea floor, it already beats Everest. (8)
VO4 But that's not the bottom. (5)
VO5 It's so heavy it pushed the sea floor down, by miles. (11)
VO6 Like a bowling ball on a mattress. (7)
VO7 Measured from its true base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall. (13)
VO8 And that turtle has no idea (6)

PRONUNCIATION. The only Hawaiian words spoken are "Mauna Loa", twice. Say MOW-nuh LOH-uh: "Mau" rhymes with "cow", and the stress falls on MAU and LO. English IPA /ˈmaʊnə ˈloʊə/; Hawaiian [ˈmɐwnɐ ˈlowɐ]. If the default read fails the phone listen test, add a pronunciation-dictionary alias: "Mauna Loa" -> "Mow-nuh Loh-uh". Confirm on wehewehe.org before the final render. These names appear only in the description, in case one is ever voiced:
- Hawaiʻi: hah-VAI-ee or hah-WAI-ee, with a glottal stop before the final "ee".
- Punaluʻu: poo-nah-LOO-oo, with a glottal stop before the last "oo".
- Kaʻū: kah-OO, with a glottal stop and a long final "oo".
- honu: HOH-noo.

result.hook:
VO at 0.00: "This beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest." It is 12 words, 4.7 s. The question opens in the first six words, "This beach is on a mountain", which land by about 1.9 s. The sentence runs past the 8-word target because the loop sentence needs the whole claim.

Frame 0 is identical to the last frame: POSE A, 1.2 km off Punaluʻu at 140 m, looking straight up the slope at Mauna Loa.
- Turquoise surf rolls onto a black-sand crescent.
- A giant paper honu (a public-domain NOAA or USFWS photo cut-out, playful paper scale) basks in the lower third.
- The green Kaʻū slopes climb to Mauna Loa's broad dome on the skyline under pale haze.
- The off-white postcard headline "ALMOST TWICE / EVEREST" hangs in the deep-blue sky.

It is already moving: the crane eases down from rest, the surf rolls and the turtle's paper edge flutters. The question it plants: Everest is the tallest mountain and this beach is at sea level, so how can that be true?
result.payoff:
From 21.3 s the crane climbs the sliced mountain from its true base while the counter rolls. The summit edge lands at the top as Rodney says "Measured from its true base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall." ABOUT / 56,000 / FEET lands on the spoken words.

The pull-back then shows the whole column. Everest stands on the same base line at VE 1.0 and reaches about halfway (52%). A second Everest drops onto the first with a thunk, and its tip just clears Mauna Loa's summit, so "almost twice" is proven on screen with no second number.

The comic payoff lands in the last 2.5 s. The sea rushes back, the camera returns to the beach, and the giant paper turtle has not moved: "And that turtle has no idea". The replay finishes the sentence: "...this beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest."

The pull-back to POSE H shows Everest on the same base reaching 52%. Then the stack gag, where a second Everest drops on and pokes just 37 px above the summit, proves "almost twice" on screen with no second number. That is a genuine payoff plus a laugh. The comic tail "And that turtle has no idea" is a good callback, and the re-landed headline card completes the joke for first-time viewers even if they never replay. Weaknesses: (1) the 3.25 s VO gap after it (see mid-drop). (2) As a funnel this Short closes every loop. It spends the long-form's final line ("Every beach ... is the very top of a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest") and its 56,000 payoff, and leaves no open question pointing to the film. The update explicitly allows one payoff Short, and the D+7 hold is the right mitigation, so this is acceptable, but expect little traffic to the long-form from it.
result.truth:
Clean, and checked against primary sources today.
- Fetched the USGS Volcano Watch "How high is Mauna Loa?". It confirms the summit at 4,170 m (13,680 ft), "flanks ... continue another 5,000 m (16,400 ft) below sea level to the sea floor", "depressed the sea floor another 8,000 m (26,000 ft)", the Moho "bowed downward by as much as 8 km (4.8 mi)", and "total relief of Mauna Loa, from its true base to its summit, is about 17,170 m (56,000 ft)".
  - So VO2 holds ("most of it is underwater": 55% measured from the sea floor, 76% measured from the true base).
  - VO3 holds: 9,170 vs 8,849 m. Showing Everest's full 8,849 m on a sea-floor pedestal is generous to Everest, so the claim is conservative.
  - VO5 "by miles" holds (about 5 mi). VO7 holds verbatim (about 56,000 ft, from its true base). "Almost twice" = 1.94.
- Point-queried the Hawaiʻi Statewide GIS geologic units layer at Punaluʻu (19.1361 N, 155.5047 W). It returns volcano "mloa", Kau Basalt, Qk1y, 3,000-5,000 yr, Wolfe and Morris 1996a. So "This beach is on a mountain" (Mauna Loa) and the description's "sits on the lava of Mauna Loa" are true.
- The one big number, the absence of on-screen sources, and the absence of any AI mention all comply.
- "Mauna Loa" pronunciation note MOW-nuh LOH-uh / [ˈmɐwnɐ ˈlowɐ] is correct. Punaluʻu, Kaʻū, Hawaiʻi and honu notes are given, and the ʻokina is used correctly in the description.
- Honesty risk in the render, not the script: the "beats Everest" margin is only 320 m, or 39 px. The visual plan says TerrainStage has a "curved hazy horizon". If the engine applies Earth curvature, the summit plane at 150 km drops about 1.77 km (about 216 px at 8.19 m/px). Everest is "drawn over the terrain" and the plan's pixel maths is flat geometry. If Everest is placed with flat maths while the terrain is curved, the error is 5x the margin and could flip or exaggerate the comparison.
- Minor: the dent animation keeps "the summit does not move" while rock "fills in behind". That is didactically fine and allowed as "plausible but schematic", but do not imply the mountain grew taller during it.
- Asset VERIFYs (PD turtle and bowling-ball photos) are correctly left open.
must_fix: HOOK AUDIO: VO1 is spliced from the subordinate clause "...has no idea this beach is on a mountain...", where "this" is normally unstressed with mid-sentence pitch. Before lock, play 0.0-2.0 s cold on a phone. If "This beach is on a mountain" does not sound like a stressed, fresh declarative, force a prosodic reset in the single take (e.g. "And that turtle has no idea... THIS beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.") or generate VO1 as its own sentence. Then re-test the "idea | this" seam over 5 loops for pitch and loudness jumps.

FIRST VISUAL EVENT IS AT 4.70 s: start the water pulling away by about 1.8-2.0 s, on "mountain". The foam rim slides back past the turtle and the surf line drops, then the full 2 s whoosh follows. The swipe window gets real motion, and frame 0 stays identical to the last frame. The 140->118 m crane drift from 1.2 km is not visible motion on a phone.

KILL THE DEAD AIR AFTER THE PAYOFF: 26.6-29.85 s has 3.25 s with no VO, including a 1.65 s 'REWIND' of undoing. Cut the rewind to about 1.0 s with a comic snap-back or crash zoom back to the beach, and start "And that turtle has no idea" about 1 s earlier, so speech resumes no more than 1.5 s after "tall". Keep the stack-gag thunk.

NUMBER BLOCK STYLE: "56,000" in yellow #FFD23F with white "ABOUT"/"FEET" on a "feathered 50% dark scrim" is the clone grammar of an accent word on a dark caption, whatever its edge softness. Drop the scrim and the yellow-accent pairing. Set ABOUT / 56,000 / FEET in this Short's own paper language (ink on an off-white #F6F1E4 card) or as plain white with stroke straight on the face, so every text element in the Short is paper and none of it is clone-style.

EVEREST PLACEMENT QC (the 39 px margin): project Everest through the SAME camera and terrain projection as Mauna Loa, including any Earth curvature TerrainStage applies (about 216 px of drop at 150 km), not with flat-geometry overlay maths. Prefer an in-scene, depth-tested mesh. On the rendered 11.3 s frame, measure that Everest's peak sits 30-45 px BELOW Mauna Loa's skyline, and on the 26.6 s hero frame that it reaches 50-54%. If the engine is curved, the pedestal base will not sit on the visible floor horizon, so let the floor occlude it rather than drawing it over the floor.

LOOP SEAM KINEMATICS: specify zero velocity at 32.40 s for vfov and pitch as well as position (the return is a dolly-zoom 12°->34°), and the matching ease-from-rest at 0.00. After the TTS retime, recompute the loop clock (surf and flutter period = final length / 6) and re-cut the surf bed to the exact final length.

FRAME-0 REALISM GATE: the 140 m beach plate (surf, black sand, the Punaluʻu palm grove, the Kaʻū slopes from a 10 m DEM plus ortho) is the engine's hardest shot, and it is the hook frame. Phone-test the middle frame with the teen panel for 'real place vs game'. If it fails, raise POSE A to an aerial oblique (about 600-1,000 m) where DEM and ortho read as real, keep the giant paper honu clearly paper, and keep the identical pose at both ends.

result.title: You Can't Walk From Maui to Lānaʻi (Unless...)
result.narration:
TEXT SENT TO TTS (ONE request, rotated so the loop seam is one natural take). Voice "Rodney - Clear Educator" (voice_id eY2VJs4Gi8QKG2RV01sS), model eleven_v4, same voice settings as the long-form, with the pronunciation dictionary "MJ-Hawaii" (built from research/ep02/script/lexicon.json) attached. Generate 3 takes and pick one by the listen test below.

Then the ice melted, the sea crept back, and ever since, you can't walk to Lānaʻi. Unless you pull the plug. Lānaʻi snaps onto Maui. Molokaʻi snaps onto Lānaʻi. Sorry, ferry. You're grounded. The Ice Age pulled this plug for real. The catch? Nobody ever walked it. People hadn't made it here yet.

53 words, all written new for this Short. It reuses none of the long-form's lines: "Drop the sea four hundred feet", "become one island", "That's not a what-if", "No ferry needed".

Estimated speech: about 19.8 s. This is calibrated on Rodney's measured take (audio/rodney_test/timing.json): about 0.19 s per syllable mid-sentence, 0.5-0.85 s on sentence-final words, comma pauses 0.08-0.15 s. The draft assumed 179 wpm; this plan does not.

HOW THE TAKE IS PLACED (build to the real take)
1. Align the chosen take to get word timings. Cut it at sentence ends, and inside the comma pause after "since,".
2. Seam placement:
   - "you can't walk to Lānaʻi." starts at 0.05.
   - "...ever since," ends so that the take's own comma pause spans the seam, plus at most 0.1 s of room tone: about 0.16 s at the end and 0.05 s at the start.
3. Lines are placed only by adding or trimming silence between sentences. No time-stretching.
4. Planned placement. These are estimates; every picture event in the table is anchored to a word and moves with it.
   - VO1 "You can't walk to Lānaʻi." 0.05-1.66
   - VO2 "Unless you pull the plug." 1.86-3.41 ("Unless" lands before 2.2 s)
   - VO3 "Lānaʻi snaps onto Maui." 4.41-6.25
   - VO4 "Molokaʻi snaps onto Lānaʻi." 6.45-8.63
   - VO5 "Sorry, ferry." 9.73-11.16, then "You're grounded." 11.71-12.69
   - VO6 "The Ice Age pulled this plug for real." 12.99-15.11
   - VO7 "The catch? Nobody ever walked it." 15.46-18.09
   - VO8 "People hadn't made it here yet." 18.39-20.32
   - VO9 "Then the ice melted, the sea crept back, and ever since," 21.28-24.84
   - Holes between lines: 0.20, 1.00 (plug drain), 0.20, 1.10 (rim and crash zoom), 0.55 (sad toot), 0.30, 0.35, 0.30, 0.96 (the comic awkward beat). None is over 1.2 s.
5. If the real take runs long:
   - First shrink the 1.00, 1.10 and 0.96 holes to 0.9, 0.9 and 0.6.
   - If speech plus the minimum holes still exceeds about 24.8 s, go to 11 bars (27.5 s). Give the extra time to those three holes (at most 1.2 s each) and to G1 (+0.5 s).
   - If the take runs short, grow those three holes up to 1.2 s.
6. Choosing the take. Listen on a phone speaker and check that:
   - every Hawaiian name is right;
   - "since," keeps a continuing comma tone;
   - played cold from 0.00, "You can't walk to Lānaʻi." sounds like an opening line, not half a sentence.

PRONUNCIATION
These are alias rules in MJ-Hawaii, the same entries as the long-form lexicon. Check every one on wehewehe.org, and with a Hawaiian speaker if possible, before the render.

Spoken by Rodney:
- Lānaʻi (said 4 times) -> alias "lah-NAH-ee". Hawaiian [laːˈnɐʔi]: a long first "ah", stress on NAH, and a light glottal catch before the final "ee". Never "luh-NYE".
- Molokaʻi -> alias "moh-loh-KAH-ee", [ˌmoloˈkɐʔi]. Never "moh-loh-KYE".
- Maui -> Rodney's default "MOW-ee", [ˈmɐwi]. Add the alias "MAO-ee" only if the listen test fails.
- Fallback: if the alias rules do not match the strings that contain the ʻokina, send the respellings in the text itself and repeat the phone-speaker listen pass.
- Captions are our own uploaded caption file with the native spellings (lexicon caption_map), never YouTube's auto-captions.

On screen only: LĀNAʻI, MAUI, MOLOKAʻI (pronunciations as above).

Description, pinned comment and tags only (Rodney never says these):
- Hawaiʻi "hah-WHY-ee" (or "hah-VAI-ee"), [həˈwɐiʔi], with a glottal catch before the last "ee".
- Kahoʻolawe "kah-hoh-oh-LAH-veh", [kəˌhoʔoˈlɐve].
- Maui Nui "MAO-ee NOO-ee" ("Big Maui").
- ʻAuʻau "ao-AO", [ʔɐuˈʔɐu]. The Grigg paper title prints it as "Au'au".

Production place names, never spoken (for the crew; rule-derived, so check on wehewehe.org):
- Launiupoko "lau-nee-oo-POH-koh"
- Lahaina "lah-HIGH-nah"
- Olowalu "oh-loh-WAH-loo"
- Lānaʻihale "lah-NAH-ee-HAH-leh"
- Kalohi "kah-LOH-hee"
- Pailolo "pie-LOH-loh"
